title: Implement `vec_identify_runs()`
description:
Part of https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/1081
Can be used to implement `vec_locate_runs()` in https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/1210
Would help with https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/5184

New `vec_identify_runs()`, which returns an integer vector of ids that identify runs in a vector. Works column-wise over data frames, which makes it very performant. The number of runs is attached as an attribute, `n`, since this is somewhat related to `vec_group_id()`, which returns the number of groups as an attribute.

``` r
library(vctrs)

set.seed(123)

# 1 million rows, 3 columns, 27 unique rows
# Random order - so lots of small runs
df <- data.frame(
  x = sample(3, 1e6, replace = TRUE),
  y = sample(3, 1e6, replace = TRUE),
  z = sample(3, 1e6, replace = TRUE)
)

# Single vectors are extremely fast
bench::mark(vec_identify_runs(df$x))[1:4]
#> # A tibble: 1 x 4
#>   expression                   min   median `itr/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>              <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl>
#> 1 vec_identify_runs(df$x)    644µs    860µs      849.

# For reference
bench::mark(rle(df$x))[1:4]
#> Warning: Some expressions had a GC in every iteration; so filtering is disabled.
#> # A tibble: 1 x 4
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl>
#> 1 rle(df$x)    42.6ms   47.8ms      19.7

# Data frames take longer than individual single vectors because it
# has to manage infrastructure for tracking runs from previous columns,
# but it is overall very fast
bench::mark(vec_identify_runs(df))[1:4]
#> # A tibble: 1 x 4
#>   expression                 min   median `itr/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>            <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl>
#> 1 vec_identify_runs(df)    9.2ms   10.7ms      94.7

attr(vec_identify_runs(df), "n")
#> [1] 962947

# Now with sorted df == longer runs
df <- vec_sort(df)

bench::mark(vec_identify_runs(df))[1:4]
#> # A tibble: 1 x 4
#>   expression                 min   median `itr/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>            <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl>
#> 1 vec_identify_runs(df)   4.78ms   5.24ms      190.

attr(vec_identify_runs(df), "n")
#> [1] 27
```

title: Fix `obj_maybe_translate_encoding()` crash
description:
Closes #1233 

The crash occurred when we had the following scenario:

- A list
- A data frame element in that list
- A rcrd column of that data frame, which has a `vec_size()` that is different from the low level `Rf_length()`

A proxy of the outer list won't proxy the elements of the list, so the rcrd column of the data frame didn't get proxied. When we eventually processed that data frame element, we assumed it had been proxied and passed the `size` of the data frame on to each column as the number of elements to iterate over. Since the rcrd wasn't proxied, the `size` didn't match up with its actual `Rf_length()` and we indexed OOB.

The fix is to treat data frames that are elements of a list as lists themselves. This forces us to compute the length of each list/character column individually with `Rf_length()`, so we correctly compute the unproxied length of the rcrd column. I think this is a more appropriate fix vs a potential alternative of proxying each list element.

I don't really expect this to have any performance impact.

I somehow forgot to add the meaningful part of the fix as its own commit, so it got tied in with the commit "Revert `size` to `n` change" 😞 , sorry. I only just noticed that.

- A rcrd column of that data frame, which has a `vec_size()` that is different from the low level `Rf_length()`

A proxy of the outer list won't proxy the elements of the list, so the rcrd column of the data frame didn't get proxied. When we eventually processed that data frame element, we assumed it had been proxied and passed the `size` of the data frame on to each column as the number of elements to iterate over. Since the rcrd wasn't proxied, the `size` didn't match up with its actual `Rf_length()` and we indexed OOB.

The fix is to treat data frames that are elements of a list as lists themselves. This forces us to compute the length of each list/character column individually with `Rf_length()`, so we correctly compute the unproxied length of the rcrd column. I think this is a more appropriate fix vs a potential alternative of proxying each list element.

I don't really expect this to have any performance impact.

title: Add `vec_slice2()` and `vec_assign2()`
description:
Branched from #1226.

Following `vec_chop2()` and `vec_map()`, this further explores the idea of "extracting" variants of vctrs primitives.

- With atomic vectors, `vec_slice2()` and `vec_assign2()` are equivalent to `vec_slice()` and `vec_assign()`. The only difference is that `vec_slice2()` zaps the names of the result.

- `vec_slice2()` with lists makes use of the list storage requirement and calls `.subset2()`.

- `vec_assign2()` with lists wraps the RHS into a list. Genericity is ensured by `vec_assign()` which coerces the RHS (now a list) to the type of the LHS (a list type). This allows the class of the LHS to initialise attributes, possibly based on the contents of the RHS.

One big difference with `[[<-` is that `NULL` values are not treated as a deletion sentinel.

```r
x <- list(foo = 1, bar = 2)

vec_assign2(x, 2, NULL)
#> $foo
#> [1] 1
#>
#> $bar
#> NULL
```

There is currently no way to remove elements:

```r
vec_assign2(x, 2, zap())
#> Error: Can't zap elements.
```

These operations are unexported for now.

title: Support long vectors in `translate.c`
description: This should be a harmless change

title: Use `df_list()` to validate fields of record vectors
description:
Branched from #1223.

- The fields of record vectors are validated with `df_list()`.
- We now use vctrs primitives in the base vector methods.

This makes record vectors more flexible (recycling of fields, allows df-cols and any vctrs types as field), simplifies internals, and will make it easier to support record lists and record data frames.

Branched from #1229.

Fixes handling of double tables and closes #1190.

title: Treat names of one-dimensional arrays consistently
description:
The `vec_names()` of arrays are now picked from the dimnames:

```r
x <- array(1:2, dimnames = list(c("a", "b")))

# Before
vec_names(x)
#> NULL

# After
vec_names(x)
#> [1] "a" "b"
```

And they are now treated as column names in `vec_rbind()`, consistently with named ordinary vectors:

```r
# Before
vec_rbind(x, x)
#>   ...1 ...2
#> 1    1    2
#> 2    1    2

# After
vec_rbind(x, x)
#>   a b
#> 1 1 2
#> 2 1 2

# Consistently with
y <- c(a = 1L, b = 2L)
vec_rbind(y, y)
#>   a b
#> 1 1 2
#> 2 1 2
```

title: Fix redundant names handling during concatenation
description:
Concatenating functions deal with outer names manually so they can apply a `name_spec`. This work is redundant with the names assignment performed in `vec_assign()`.

To fix this, we now have `ignore_outer_names` in the `struct vec_assign_opts` to indicate that outer names will be handled elsewhere but vec-assign should still handle inner names.

title: Recycle return value of `name_spec` instead of arguments
description:
Branched from #1219
Closes #1099

Don't recycle the `outer` argument of name specifications.

- It's more intuitive for name-spec implementor since the outer name is unique.
- It's more flexible, name-spec can now return a single name to be recycled.

title: Allow returning `NULL` names from a `name_spec`
description:
Branched from #1218.
Closes #1215.

This makes it possible to return `NULL` from a `name_spec`. The names vector of the concatenated vector is never allocated or assigned if the name-spec only returns `NULL`. To achieve this, the names vectors are lazily allocated.

This will be useful for implementing `purrr::flatten()` in a backward-compatible way (tidyverse/purrr#785).

The internals of `vec_c()`, `vec_unchop()` with supplied indices, and `vec_rbind()` are now a little more symmetric in style, naming, and structure.

title: Fix excessive duplication during concatenation of named vectors
description:
* Add `vec_proxy_set_names()` which takes a `vctrs_owned` argument. This variant of `vec_set_names()` never dispatches and uses `vec_clone_referenced(x, owned)` instead of `r_clone_referenced()`.

```r
ints <- rep(list(set_names(1:3, letters[1:3])), 1e4)
bench::mark(
  base = unlist(ints),
  vctrs = vec_unchop(ints),
  check = FALSE
)[1:8]
#> # Before
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` n_itr  n_gc
#> 1 base        669.7µs  843.4µs  1101.     351.66KB     7.82   563     4
#> 2 vctrs          1.5s     1.5s     0.667    2.24GB    29.3      1    44

#> # After
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` n_itr  n_gc
#> 1 base       663.31µs 833.14µs     1203.     352KB    10.9    554     5
#> 2 vctrs        4.52ms   4.93ms      201.     625KB     4.18    96     2
```

* Don't repair row names on proxies. Instead, row names are now repaired as part of restoration of data frames.

```r
df <- new_data_frame(
  df_list(
    x = as.list(1:2),
    y = 1:2
  ),
  row.names = c("foo", "bar")
)
dfs <- rep(list(df), 3)
vec_unchop(dfs)

dfs <- rep(list(df), 1e2)
bench::mark(
  vctrs = vec_unchop(dfs),
  check = FALSE
)[1:8]
#> # Before
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` n_itr  n_gc
#> 1 vctrs         449ms    635ms      1.57    85.4MB     1.57     2     2

#> # After
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` n_itr  n_gc
#> 1 vctrs         905µs   1.04ms      948.    14.8KB     18.0   421     8
```

This issue isn't fixed in the case of df-cols because we proxy and restore these at each assignment. This particular bug is tracked in #1217 and will be solved once #1107 is resolved.

We are now tracking memory allocations with human readable sizes in golden tests. This should allow us to detect memory issues early.

This PR also imports the pairlist and attributes utils from the rlang C library. This is because I initially tried to solve the names duplication issue with `r_clone_shared()`. The attribute getters from the GNU R lib are problematic in that regard because they max-bump the namedness/refcount of attributes. I don't think this is appropriate behaviour because in most cases we are only inspecting the attribute. The rlang utils never bump refcounts, and they also never allocate (no need for protection). Even though these rlang utils are no longer necessary to fix the duplication issues since I switched to the `vctrs_owned` approach that Davis introduced, I kept them in the PR because they have better properties.

title: Remove proxy check in `vec_is_list()`
description:
Part of #1208 

The proxy check was originally suggested here https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/pull/1003#issuecomment-612883620. I am not convinced that we need it, and it would help with list-rcrds outlined in #1208 to remove it.

I really like how simple `vec_is_list()` is now. It is very easy to explain.

Internally, we do not currently use `vec_is_list()` in any way that could cause issues after removing this restriction. We never proxy `x` after checking that it is a list with `vec_is_list()`. We only use it in:

- `vec_unchop()` to check that `x` is a list
- `vec_unchop()` to check that `indices` is a list
- `list_sizes()` to check that `x` is a list

I think all of these are valid and safe uses of `vec_is_list()`

title: Call `vec_cast()` instead of `vec_cast_common()` in `vec_c()`
description:
To avoid an extra list allocation:

```r
c(
  ints = with_memory_prof(vec_unchop(ints)),
  dbls = with_memory_prof(vec_unchop(dbls)),
  ints_to_int = with_memory_prof(vec_unchop(ints, ptype = int())),
  dbls_to_int = with_memory_prof(vec_unchop(dbls, ptype = int()))
)

## Before
#>        ints        dbls ints_to_int dbls_to_int
#>        1744        2144        1744        1744

## After
#>        ints        dbls ints_to_int dbls_to_int
#>         896        1296         896         896
```

Doesn't impact performance but it seems tidier to avoid allocs unless needed so we don't wonder about it. I added a note at the allocation site of the vec-size cache to mention the extra alloc does improve performance.

Added golden tests to measure the memory allocated during concatenation. `vec_c()` has a bunch of extra allocs which should be resolved with r-lib/rlang#937.

title: Add a user FAQ about scalar type errors
Implement `data_frame()`
description:
Closes #1198 
Closes #1199 (an alternative to that PR)

This PR beefs up the existing internal `data_frame()` helper and exports it.

A few new features:

- `.size` argument
- `.name_repair` argument
- Tidy recycling of columns (which makes it safer to use too)
- Fully unnamed inputs are automatically given `""` for column names to prevent creation of corrupt data frames
- Auto-splicing of unnamed data frames
- Dynamic dots

Altogether this gives a pretty performant data frame constructor that follows tidyverse semantics.

title: Avoid calling `STRING_ELT()` on unnamed data frames
description:
Closes #1198 

Simple adjustment to `df_flatten_loop()` to avoid extracting names from an unnamed data frame.

Even with unnamed data frames, we return a data frame from `df_flatten()` that at least has `""` as column names. This makes it easy to ensure proper behavior in the edge case where an unnamed data frame has a df-col that has names (this is `df3` in the added tests)

title: Add a user FAQ about type compatibility
Cleanup TRUELENGTHs with `R_ExecWithCleanup()`
description:
This PR uses `R_ExecWithCleanup()` in two places to more safely reset truelengths of CHARSXPs.

`chr_order()` is used to process either a single character vector or the first column of a data frame if it is a character vector. I've now wrapped the implementation of this function in `R_ExecWithCleanup()`, and the cleanup function calls `truelength_reset()`. If we are ordering a character vector and a longjump occurs (due to allocation failure or an internal error), this ensures that the truelengths get reset on exit.

For `df_order()`, when a character column is encountered we normally mark the truelengths of the entire column, process the chunks, and then reset the entire column before moving on to the next column. It is possible that a longjump could occur while processing the chunks. The easiest thing to do here was to wrap all of `df_order()` in `R_ExecWithCleanup()`. The cleanup function again calls `truelength_reset()`. When there are no character columns, this is essentially a no-op. When there are character columns in the data frame, but their truelengths got reset properly, this is again a no-op. It really only does something if we are in the middle of processing a character column and a longjump occurs.

Update: Oops, opened this on the wrong branch

```r
  CHAR() can only be applied to a 'CHARSXP', not a 'character'
```

title: When restoring unnamed data frames, repair column names with `""`
description:
Previously we had this untested behavior:

```r
> vec_slice(new_data_frame(list(1)), 1)
  NA
1  1
> names(vec_slice(new_data_frame(list(1)), 1))
[1] NA
```

This came from the df-restore code path, which tried to set the names to `character()`, but `Rf_setAttrib()` extended that with `Rf_lengthgets()` to the length of the data frame, and it "extends" with `NA_character_`.

I think that the names should be "repaired" to the empty string here. Now:

```r
> vec_slice(new_data_frame(list(1)), 1)
   
1 1
> names(vec_slice(new_data_frame(list(1)), 1))
[1] ""
```

title: Revert to a simpler ownership model - but always duplicate ALTREP
description:
Closes tidyverse/dplyr#5327
Closes #1124
Closes #1122 

Reverts back to a slightly simpler ownership model of `VCTRS_OWNED_true` and `VCTRS_OWNED_false`.

When we own the object, we only ever attempt to duplicate it if it is ALTREP. If `vec_init()` ever creates ALTREP objects in the future (https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/pull/837), this will be required. When doing assignment, we have to duplicate ALTREP objects before dereferencing even if we own them, because we need access to the actual data that it is representing, not the ALTREP object's internals.

When we don't own the object, we use `r_clone_referenced()` to determine if we need to duplicate or not.

This fixed the repeated duplication that was occurring in `df_assign()`'s calls to `vec_proxy_assign_opts()`, but I then discovered that we still had repeated duplication in `vec_restore()`. To fix that, I had to borrow from the ideas in #1124 and pass through `owned` to `vec_restore()` as well. This allows us to avoid attempting duplication here as well.

With both of those in place, tidyverse/dplyr#5327 is fixed:

```r
library(dplyr)

date_frame <- tibble(date = rep(lubridate::date("2020-01-01"), 100))
date_frames_to_bind <- rep(list(date_frame), 10000)
bench::mark(bind_rows(date_frames_to_bind))
#> Warning: Some expressions had a GC in every iteration; so filtering is disabled.
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression                          min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>                     <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 bind_rows(date_frames_to_bind)    133ms    142ms      6.87    8.39MB     25.8
```

---

It is worth noting that @lionel- and I both think that eventually we should probably have recursive proxy and restore functions (https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/1107). This would allow `df_assign()` to not have to proxy and restore the output columns repeatedly, which is where many of these duplication issues arise. That would also allow us to remove the `owned` argument from `vec_restore()` again, which I am currently viewing as a temporary fix.

---

This also closes #1124, because it fixes the original problem there where columns of df-cols were being duplicated.

title: Pass `ownership` through to `vec_restore()`
description:
Closes #1122 

This PR fixes the `vec_rbind()` performance regression seen in #1122 by passing along the ownership parameter to `vec_restore()`. The sole purpose of this is to allow us to swap between `r_clone_shared()` and `r_clone_referenced()` here:

https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/pull/1124/files#diff-90e5f87281649d48864c579abd8649c3R31-R35

The problem in #1122 is that df-cols created by `vec_init()` automatically get a refcount of 1 due to the `SET_VECTOR_ELT()` call that places them in the outer data frame. When `vec_restore()` is called from `df_assign()` on those inner df-cols it eventually hands off to `vec_bare_df_restore_impl()` which unconditionally called `r_clone_referenced()`. Because our df-col _was_ referenced, it makes a shallow duplicate of it even though it is the freshly created output object. The problem with this is that by shallow duplicating the df-col, the refcount of all the columns in the df-col gets bumped from 1 to 2. So on the next iteration of `vec_rbind()`, those columns get shallow duplicated (which is really a full duplication for non-lists). That was where the performance really suffered.

By passing the ownership parameter through, we can correctly switch to `r_clone_shared()` when restoring, which allows in place modification of the case where the refcount is 1. Since the df-col's refcount is 1, it doesn't get shallow duplicated and the inner columns of that df-col don't have their refcount bumped.

This is on R 4.0 with this PR. We now match R 3.6 performance 

```r
library(vctrs)

df_col <- new_data_frame(list(x = 1:2))
df <- new_data_frame(list(y = df_col))

x <- rep_len(list(df), 10000)
y <- rep_len(list(df_col), 10000)

lst_rbind <- function(x) {
    vec_rbind(!!!x)
}

bench::mark(lst_rbind(x))
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression        min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>   <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 lst_rbind(x)   37.8ms   39.1ms      25.6     278KB     44.7
```

---

In theory this needs a test, but I'm not really sure how to design one for this pathological case

title: Let `vec_proxy_compare()` unwrap 1 col dfs and flatten df-cols
description:
Follow up to #1142

- We now handle `vec_proxy_compare()` from C in a similar way to `vec_proxy_equal()`. We recurse over data frame columns, dispatching to the R level `vec_proxy_compare()` as we go. This also now uses the `df_flatten()` and `vec_proxy_unwrap()` infrastructure.

- I currently have a separate `vec_proxy_compare_recursive()` function, but it could be removed if we eventually remove `relax` entirely in favor of always seeing lists as orderable using `seq_along()`. Then we could just go through `vec_proxy_recursive()`

title: Fix fallback rbind
description:
Branched from #1104.

* Add a new common class fallback option in the coercion mechanism. The options are wrapped in a struct and a structured `list()` which can be passed back and forth between the R and C sides.

* When this fallback is turned on, the common class suffix is collected by `vec_ptype_common()`, and stored in a sentinel ptype. This sentinel is not meant to be leaked to users. With the current design, the fallback should only be used through higher level operations like `vec_cast_common()` or `vec_rbind()`. We may be able to find a more general approach for 0.4.0.

* `vec_cast_common()` leaves untouched the inputs which have a fallback.

* `vec_c()` and `vec_rbind()` call `base::c()` if inputs have a fallback common class and implement a `c()` method. There are still several cases which are not handled well, and the rbind code needs to be refactored. We'll do this for 0.4.0 as part of the switch to recursive proxying and restoration.

* The special-casing of sfc lists has been removed, and we fall back to `c.sfc()` instead. Fixes r-spatial/sf#1390.

Adapting `vec_match()` to use this fallback will be a simple matter of using a fallback-enabled variant of `vec_cast_common()`.

`vec_unchop()` will be adapted to the new fallback in a different PR.

title: Fix unspecified fallback
description:
Branched from #1111.

This adds support for combining unspecified chunks to the `base::c()` fallback. We can't rely on `c()` for this because implementations might not handle unspecified inputs, and if unspecified is the first input this would prevent dispatch from reaching the expected method. Instead, we first combine non-unspecified chunks, then use `[` with `NA` integer locations to expand the result with missing values.

With this change, the fallback is now consistent when disjoint data frames are binded: 

```r
x <- sf::st_sfc(sf::st_point(1:2))
y <- sf::st_sfc(sf::st_multipoint(matrix(1:4, 2)), sf::st_multipoint(matrix(5:8, 2)))

vec_rbind(
  data_frame(x = x),
  data_frame(y = y)
)
#>             x                         y
#> 1 POINT (1 2)          MULTIPOINT EMPTY
#> 2 POINT EMPTY MULTIPOINT ((1 3), (2 4))
#> 3 POINT EMPTY MULTIPOINT ((5 7), (6 8))
```

title: Add faster `df_cast_loop()` path to `df_cast_opts()`
description:
Closes #1070 

Adds a fast path to `df_cast_opts()` when `x` and `to` have the same names. Very similar to `df_ptype2()`. Speed up is ~2x when the fast path is used, but I could see this being a very common case.

---


These examples take 10000 data frames of different types and cast them to the same common type.

``` r
library(vctrs)

vec_cast_common_lst <- function(x) {
  vec_cast_common(!!!x)
}
```

These all share the same `names()` SEXP, and the fast path is used.

```r
x <- rep_len(list(data.frame(x = 1, y = 2)), 10000)

# master
bench::mark(vec_cast_common_lst(x), iterations = 100)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression                  min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>             <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_cast_common_lst(x)   15.5ms   19.9ms      49.5     160KB     33.0

# this PR
bench::mark(vec_cast_common_lst(x), iterations = 100)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression                  min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>             <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_cast_common_lst(x)   7.84ms    9.3ms      105.     160KB     21.5
```

These all have different `names()` SEXP, and the fast path is used.

```r
y <- replicate(10000, data.frame(x = 1, y = 2), simplify = FALSE)

# master
bench::mark(vec_cast_common_lst(y), iterations = 100)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression                  min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>             <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_cast_common_lst(y)   22.2ms   27.7ms      35.5     156KB     34.1

# this PR
bench::mark(vec_cast_common_lst(y), iterations = 100)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression                  min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>             <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_cast_common_lst(y)   14.8ms   18.3ms      55.6     156KB     16.6
```

Introduction of `z` forces a common type of `df<x, y, z, w>`, so now none of the data frames will use the fast path. This is mainly to show that there is minimal overhead in this approach when it isn't used.

```r
z <- data.frame(z = 1, w = 2)
z <- c(list(z), x)

# master
bench::mark(vec_cast_common_lst(z), iterations = 100)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression                  min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>             <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_cast_common_lst(z)   29.4ms   51.6ms      20.5     156KB     55.0

# this PR
bench::mark(vec_cast_common_lst(z), iterations = 100)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression                  min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>             <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_cast_common_lst(z)     35ms   52.8ms      20.6     156KB     178.
```

title: Refine `vec_assign()` ownership semantics
description:
Follow up to #1062 

This PR refines the ownership model of `vec_assign()`. It changes from a boolean ownership model to one with 3 states: owned, shared, or unknown.

It works similarly to how it was set up before, except for calls to `vec_proxy_assign_opts()`. Now, if `vec_proxy_assign_opts()` is called with `vctrs_ownership_unknown` then it will attempt to determine the ownership for the data structure by a call to `NO_REFERENCES()` on the proxy. If there are no references, it is owned.

This change helps with slider. If slider creates a data frame at the C level and then calls `vec_proxy_assign()` to fill it, a default of `vctrs_ownership_unknown` is assumed. But `NO_REFERENCES(proxy)` will be true on the fresh data frame, so the ownership is updated to `vctrs_ownership_owned`. The columns of the data frame are all passed this updated ownership value, so no copies are made.

In the obscure case where we create a data frame at the C level, and then set one of the columns in this freshly created data frame to be a vector that is already referenced somewhere else, we are still safe. Assigning into that fresh data frame will use `vctrs_ownership_owned`, which will be passed on to each column, but columns that are also referenced elsewhere will have a refcount of at least 2. One from being referenced elsewhere, and one from being set in this fresh data frame. So `r_maybe_duplicate_shared()` will copy it as needed to not modify it by reference accidentally. But again, I don't see this case ever arising.

Fix performance in R 4.0.0
description:
Closes #838 

Requires https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/pull/963 to ensure that the NAMEDNESS of captured `...` is always set to the max value.

Unfortunately R 4.0.0 is going to cause a huge performance regression to `vec_rbind()`. It is very similar to the problem in https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/984

Here is current master, with R 4.0.0. This is supposed to take ~20ms.

```r
library(vctrs)
library(tibble)

x <- rep(list(data.frame(x = 1)), 10000)

fn <- function(x) {
  vec_rbind(!!!x)
}

# master
bench::mark(fn(x), iterations = 10)
#> Warning: Some expressions had a GC in every iteration; so filtering is disabled.
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 fn(x)         285ms    311ms      3.12     764MB     54.2

# this PR
bench::mark(fn(x), iterations = 10)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 fn(x)        19.8ms   21.7ms      43.0     200KB     18.4
```

The performance regression here is basically the same as in https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/984, in `df_assign()` we are making a copy of the final output container every time we assign one of the 10000 data frames into it.

The main issue is that `SET_VECTOR_ELT()` now bumps the refcnt of the `value` you are assigning, where it didn't used to do that. This makes `MAYBE_REFERENCED()` return true more often, in cases where we really don't need to make a duplicate. The fix is to switch to `MAYBE_SHARED()`, but also requires a patch to rlang on R < 4.0.0 to ensure that the result of rlang's `rlang_env_dots_list()` C callable returns the captured `...` with max namedness. This is important because it forces us to always copy the dots so we don't accidentally modify by reference (the copying was already happening when we were using `MAYBE_REFERENCED()`).

I've left very detailed notes about this in one of the tests
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/pull/1057/files#diff-51c944df297abe15044974191b4f4ebbR593-R627

title: Remove `"list"` base class from list-of
description:
Reverts part of #1003 

After speaking with @lionel-, it seems that adding a base `"list"` class to list-of might not be the best idea in the long run. In the future, we might allow classes that explicitly inherit from a base type to be coercible to those base types automatically, but we probably wouldn't want that with list-ofs (we want them to be strict and not lose information easily).

This required tweaking `vec_is_list()` to know about `vctrs_list_of` and allow explicit inheritance from `"vctrs_list_of"` to be a sufficient condition for being a list.

This additionally required that `new_vctr()` be less strict about `inherit_base_type = FALSE` with list input. We need to do this in `new_list_of()`. Separately, this is also how we would create list-vctrs that are treated as atomic vectors. `numeric_version` is one such example of this. It is implemented internally as a list, but it should not be treated as one. So `vec_is()` should return `TRUE`, but `vec_is_list()` should return `FALSE`.

title: Handle different column specs in df fallback

* Restore attributes if there is no `[` implementation, so that we can give a proper warning about implementing ptype2 methods.

```r
df1 <- data.table::data.table(x = 1, y = 2)
df2 <- data.table::data.table(x = 3)

# Before
dplyr::bind_rows(df1, df2)
#>   x  y
#> 1 1  2
#> 2 3 NA
#> Warning message:
#> Can't combine <data.table> and <data.table>.
#> ✖ Some attributes are incompatible.
#> ℹ The author of the class should implement vctrs methods.
#> ℹ See <https://vctrs.r-lib.org/reference/faq-error-incompatible-attributes.html>.
#> ℹ Falling back to <data.frame>.


# After
dplyr::bind_rows(df1, df2)
#>    x  y
#> 1: 1  2
#> 2: 3 NA
```

title: Improve data frame coercion errors and warnings
description:
Branched from #1026.

When two data frame classes are incompatible because of their class but not because of their columns, the structure of columns no longer appear in the error message.

```r
df <- data.frame(x = 1, y = "")
foo <- structure(df, class = c("vctrs_foo", "data.frame"))
bar <- structure(df, class = c("vctrs_bar", "data.frame"))
```

Before:

```r
vec_cast(foo, bar)
#> Error: Can't convert <vctrs_foo<
#>   x: double
#>   y: character
#> >> to <vctrs_bar<
#>   x: double
#>   y: character
#> >>.
```

After:

```r
vec_cast(foo, bar)
#> Error: Can't convert <vctrs_foo[,2]> to <vctrs_bar[,2]>.
```

title: Explain why classes are incompatible
description:
We currently have this confusing error message when the is-same-class fallback fails because of diverging attribtues.

```r
vec_cast(foobar(1, bar = TRUE), foobar(2, baz = TRUE))
#> Error: Can't convert <vctrs_foobar> to <vctrs_foobar>.

vec_ptype2(foobar(1, bar = TRUE), foobar(2, baz = TRUE))
#> Error: Can't combine <vctrs_foobar> and <vctrs_foobar>.
```

With this PR, we explain the attributes are incompatible and refer to a FAQ.

```r
vec_cast(foobar(1, bar = TRUE), foobar(2, baz = TRUE))
#> Error: Can't convert <vctrs_foobar> to <vctrs_foobar>.
#> ✖ Some attributes are incompatible.
#> ℹ The author of the class should implement vctrs methods.
#> ℹ See <https://vctrs.r-lib.org/reference/faq-error-incompatible-attributes.html>.

vec_ptype2(foobar(1, bar = TRUE), foobar(2, baz = TRUE))
#> Error: Can't combine <vctrs_foobar> and <vctrs_foobar>.
#> ✖ Some attributes are incompatible.
#> ℹ The author of the class should implement vctrs methods.
#> ℹ See <https://vctrs.r-lib.org/reference/faq-error-incompatible-attributes.html>.
```

The FAQ is not written yet. This is tracked in #1016.

title: Remove internal usage of vctrs_vctr/rcrd/list_of
description:
Related to https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/968#issuecomment-611092692

This PR does two things:

- C level special casing of `vctrs_vctr`, `vctrs_list_of` and `vctrs_rcrd` has been removed. All handling of these classes is done at the R level in such a way that they could now live in an entirely different package if they wanted to (with the exception of the 1 call to `vctrs_cast()` in `vec_default_cast()`, which we will revisit elsewhere)

- In the process, I learned that `vec_is_list()` is not implemented quite right. I had to do something here, so I've changed it to first take the proxy, then check if that proxy either directly inherits from `"list"` or is a bare list.

---

The above point about `vec_is_list()` was discussed on slack, and we didn't come to a complete agreement on what the solution should be, so it is open to discussion.

The problem is that one of the ways an object can be considered a list is if:

“x is an S3 list that vec_is() returns TRUE for. For this to return TRUE, the class must implement a vec_proxy() method.”

This works nicely for `vctrs_list_of,` but it implies that `vctrs_rcrd` and `POSIXlt` should both return `TRUE` from `vec_is_list()` because they both have `vec_proxy()` methods, but I don’t think that we want that.

The proposed change uses the following rules for `vec_is_list()`:

- x is a bare list with no class
- x is a list explicitly inheriting from `"list"`
- x is an S3 object that implements a `vec_proxy()` method, and the proxy satisfies one of the above two rules

A few more notes:

- Using the proxy means that S3 types that aren't internally a list can still be considered as lists if their proxy returns a list.
- This means that S3 lists that want to be considered lists should `unclass()` in the proxy
- One alternative suggested by @lionel- is to make `vec_is_list()` generic. One problem with that that he noted is that we might end up in a scenario where an object declares itself as a list even if internally it isn't. This could cause problems in vctrs methods like `vec_unchop()`. The proxy implementation guards against this by checking the `TYPEOF(proxy)` first, so even if the user lies and attaches an explicit `"list"` class on their non-list proxy, it will return `FALSE`

title: Add fallback for foreign data frame classes
description:
Closes #981 

The warning is thrown during the ptype2 reduction. A sentinel data frame class avoids repeat warnings. I haven't implemented a fallback in `vec_cast()` because it isn't necessary for `vec_cbind()` and `vec_rbind()`.

```r
foo <- structure(mtcars[1:3], class = c("foo", "data.frame"))
bar <- structure(mtcars[9:11], class = c("bar", "data.frame"))

vec_ptype_common(foo, bar)
#> [1] mpg  cyl  disp am   gear carb
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
#> Warning: Can't combine <foo> and <bar>.
#> i vctrs coercion methods should be implemented for these classes.
#> i Falling back to <data.frame>.
```

The warning should eventually refer to a FAQ about normalising inputs to `data.frame`. This is tracked in #1016.

title: Zap input names by default in `vec_rbind()`
description:
Part of #966

`.names_to` is set to `rlang::zap()` by default. This is a sentinel for ignoring the input names.

title: Date / Datetime improvements
description:
Closes #535
Closes #561 

This PR adds a number of date / datetime improvements.

- Constructors are faster
   - And now have a small suite of tests to ensure their behaviors are correct
- Casting in the trivial cases is faster
- R level casting now uses `stop_native_implementation()`
   - Except where we need to fallback for lossy errors
- Proxying is faster
- A few bugs were fixed

Constructor:

```r
bench::mark(
  date = new_date(),
  datetime = new_datetime(),
  check = FALSE
)

# Master
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 date         7.82µs    9.5µs   102145.    8.68KB     81.8
#> 2 datetime        9µs   12.3µs    73829.   15.53KB     29.5

# This PR
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 date          976ns   1.26µs   772226.    6.17KB     77.2
#> 2 datetime     1.14µs   1.33µs   718756.     4.1KB     71.9
```

Proxy:

```r
x <- new_date()
y <- new_datetime()

bench::mark(
  date = vec_proxy(x),
  datetime = vec_proxy(y),
  check = FALSE
)

# Master
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 date         1.71µs   2.03µs   441019.      12KB     44.1
#> 2 datetime    11.64µs  14.83µs    66387.    5.54KB     19.9

# This PR
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 date         1.71µs   2.29µs   415592.    8.28KB      0

```

Casting (doing nothing)

```r
bench::mark(

  datetime_datetime = vec_cast(y, y),
  check = FALSE
)

# Master
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression             min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>        <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 date_date           3.05µs   4.06µs   240986.    4.46KB     24.1
#> 2 datetime_datetime  38.29µs  47.62µs    20565.   87.21KB     25.0

# This PR

#>   expression             min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>        <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 date_date            798ns    986ns   940620.        0B     94.1
#> 2 datetime_datetime    862ns   1.01µs   950229.        0B      0
```

Size:

```r
ct <- new_datetime(0)
lt <- as.POSIXlt(ct)

bench::mark(
  vec_size(ct),
  vec_size(lt),
  iterations = 100000
)

# Master
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression        min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>   <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>

# This PR
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression        min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>   <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_size(ct)   1.58µs   2.39µs   406129.    14.6KB    106. 
#> 2 vec_size(lt)   2.43µs   2.93µs   314628.    11.1KB     28.3
```

Datetime constructor is stricter now, requires double input (like `new_date()`)

```r
# always required double input
new_date(1L)
#> Error: `x` must be a double vector.

# stricter now
new_datetime(1L)
#> Error: `x` must be a double vector.
```

Bug: Can't convert POSIXct to Date unless it is offset with the correct UTC offset

```r
# Master

x <- as.POSIXct("2019-01-01", tz = "America/New_York")
vec_cast(x, new_date())
#> Error: Can't convert from <datetime<America/New_York>> to <date> due to loss of precision.
#> * Locations: 1

x <- as.POSIXct("2018-12-31 19:00:00", tz = "America/New_York")
vec_cast(x, new_date())
#> [1] "2019-01-01"

# This PR
x <- as.POSIXct("2019-01-01", tz = "America/New_York")
vec_cast(x, new_date())
#> [1] "2019-01-01"

x <- as.POSIXct("2018-12-31 19:00:00", tz = "America/New_York")
vec_cast(x, new_date())
#> Error: Can't convert from <datetime<America/New_York>> to <date> due to loss of precision.
#> * Locations: 1
```

Bug: POSIXlt to POSIXlt conversion didn't change time zones

```r
# Master
x <- as.POSIXlt("2019-01-01", tz = "America/New_York")
to <- as.POSIXlt(new_datetime(tzone = "America/Los_Angeles"))
vec_cast(x, to)
#> [1] "2019-01-01 EST"

# This PR
x <- as.POSIXlt("2019-01-01", tz = "America/New_York")
to <- as.POSIXlt(new_datetime(tzone = "America/Los_Angeles"))
vec_cast(x, to)
#> [1] "2018-12-31 21:00:00 PST"
```

title: Move ptype2 shape handling to C
description:
This PR moves the common shape handling in `vec_ptype2()` down to C. This has the nice benefit of allowing us to mark the R level ptype2 methods for bare types with `stop_native_implementation()`.

- New `dim.c` and `dim.h` to hold dim specific functions, and make a few of the performance critical ones inline. This aligns better with `dim.R` too.

- New `shape.c` and `shape.h` to hold the common shape functionality

   - The idea of "shape" is tweaked slightly. It is now the dimensions vector with the first axis set to 0. It used to be all of the axes except the first, but this was a little harder to build on.

   - `vec_shape2()` is the main function here, it takes two sets of dimensions to find a common shape for and returns that common shape (as defined above). It replaces `shape_common()`.

   - `vec_shaped_ptype()` replaces `shape_match()` and is the entry point that `vec_ptype2()` uses. It computes the common shape from `x` and `y` and applies it to the `ptype`.

- When I added in the `stop_native_implementation()`, I learned that the complex methods were missing from `vec_ptype2_switch_native()`. I added them.

I detect essentially 0 loss of performance for non-shaped inputs.

```r
library(vctrs)

x <- 1
y <- 1

# Master
bench::mark(vec_ptype2(x, y), iterations = 1000000)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression            min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>       <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_ptype2(x, y)    673ns    866ns  1076072.        0B     107.

# This PR
bench::mark(vec_ptype2(x, y), iterations = 1000000)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression            min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>       <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_ptype2(x, y)    699ns    875ns  1071231.        0B     107.
```

Really nice performance now for array common types

```r
library(vctrs)

x <- array(1, dim = c(2, 1, 4, 6))
y <- array(1, dim = c(3, 5, 1, 6))

# Master
bench::mark(vec_ptype2(x, y), iterations = 100000)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression            min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>       <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_ptype2(x, y)   19.9µs   23.4µs    39464.    99.1KB     54.5

# This PR
bench::mark(vec_ptype2(x, y), iterations = 100000)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression            min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>       <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_ptype2(x, y)    935ns   1.31µs   744330.        0B     89.3
```

title: Add `x_arg` to `vec_ptype()`
description:
This PR follows up on the notes in #823 and gives `vec_ptype()` an `x_arg` argument.

I also took the chance to finally switch `vec_type()` to `vec_ptype()` internally.

The nicest thing about this is a small simplification to `vec_ptype2()`, where we no longer have to do a `vec_assert()` that is guarded by a `!vec_is_partial()` before calling `vec_ptype()`. Because of #823, `vec_ptype()` handles partial types, base R scalars (like `quote(x)`), and classed scalars (like `foobar()`) correctly. Now that we can pass the `x_arg` through to `vec_ptype()`, we don't need this check anymore.

title: Add fast path for identically named data frames in `df_ptype2()`
description:
Closes #979 

This PR adds early exits for `df_ptype2()` when the names of the two data frames are either the exact same reference or have identical names. 

``` r
library(vctrs)
library(tibble)
library(rlang)
```

Empty tibble

```r
x <- tibble()

# Master
bench::mark(vec_ptype2(x, x), iterations = 100000)

```

```r
y <- as_tibble_row(set_names(as.list(1:100), paste0("a", 1:100)))

# Master
bench::mark(vec_ptype2(y, y), iterations = 100000)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6

```

Same as before, but different objects with the same names so we have to loop through the names to check that they are identical.

```r
z1 <- as_tibble_row(set_names(as.list(1:100), paste0("a", 1:100)))
z2 <- as_tibble_row(set_names(as.list(1:100), paste0("a", 1:100)))
```

title: Throw type errors from `vec_cast()`
description:
Part of #969 

- Removes all usage of `stop_incompatible_cast()` in favor of `stop_incompatible_type()`

- Adds an `action` argument to `stop_incompatible_type()` to customize the error depending on whether it is thrown from ptype2 or cast

   - In the process, this changed the current `vec_ptype2()` message

Questions:

- @lionel-, you mentioned throwing incompatible type errors for _unimplemented_ cast methods, but I feel like it makes sense to throw them for methods that are implemented as well if they just throw the error. That is what I did here.

- Related to the above point, we no longer use `stop_incompatible_cast()` anywhere. Should it be soft-deprecated?

- Right now this requires exporting this new `action` argument in `stop_incompatible_type()`. Would it be better to keep `stop_incompatible_type()` untouched and add internal `stop_incompatible_type_combine()` and `stop_incompatible_type_convert()` functions? `stop_incompatible_type()` would just call `stop_incompatible_type_combine()` but that way we don't export the new argument.

title: Return immediately if restoring to the same reference
description:
Fixes #984 

This problem was really difficult to track down.

Right now, `vec_c()` and `vec_rbind()` do the right thing with row names because of this forced shallow duplication in `df_assign()`.

https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/fd249275c79ccd01910c947f63296ea9c5e6aa99/src/slice-assign.c#L341

The problem is that this is very slow, and should be unnecessary since `out` is a completely new object that we are assigning to, so we shouldn't have to duplicate the columns.

However, naively replacing that line with `r_maybe_duplicate()` or removing it entirely results in this problem where we lose row names:

```r
library(vctrs)
library(tibble)

df_x <- new_data_frame(list(x = 1:3), row.names = letters[1:3])
df_y <- new_data_frame(list(x = 4L), row.names = "d")

x <- tibble(dfcol = df_x)
y <- tibble(dfcol = df_y)

vec_rbind(x, y)$dfcol
#> New names:
#> * `` -> ...4
#> New names:
#> * `` -> ...1
#> * `` -> ...2
#> * `` -> ...3
#>   x
#> 1 1
#> 2 2
#> 3 3
#> 4 4
```

We lose them at the `vec_restore()` step here
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/fd249275c79ccd01910c947f63296ea9c5e6aa99/src/slice-assign.c#L344

Note that in the call to `vec_restore()`, `assigned` and `out_elt` _are the same object_. This eventually passes through to `vec_restore_default()`. So when we get to this part of `vec_restore_default()` posted below we clear the attributes on `x` (`assigned`) by replacing them with `attrib`, which are the attributes of `to` (`out_elt`) but without a few of the core attributes, like the class. But because `x` and `to` are the same object, _this reset `to` as well_. So when we do the `is_data_frame(to)` check later on to decide if we should add row names on, it fails because `to` no longer has a class.

https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/fd249275c79ccd01910c947f63296ea9c5e6aa99/src/proxy-restore.c#L72-L82

I've fixed this for now by returning early from `vec_restore_default()` if we encounter identical objects. @lionel- does this seem like a reasonable fix?

title: Add dplyr methods
description:
Branched from #950.

Because `grouped_df` no longer inherit from the `tbl_df` methods, dplyr methods need to be implemented. With this PR all dplyr tests pass, except for those that count the number of regroups.

`vec_cbind()` with data frames that have special columns was problematic. One goal of frame API PRs was to find semantics that would allow propagating these special columns in colwise combinations. This is too involved for dplyr 1.0, so we use a different approach here:

- All inputs are converted to frame prototypes, i.e. zero-column inputs. `vec_restore()` is called as part of this conversion. I'm not entirely happy about using restore for this because this isn't what it was designed for. I'm not sure how we could do better, except by calling back the R level `[` method. Maybe that's a safer option.

- The restore method for `grouped_df` returns a simple tibble when the grouping columns have been lost, so the frame prototype of grouped data frames are tibbles.

- The common type is determined from the frame prototypes.

As a result, `vec_cbind(gdf, df)` returns a tibble (the simplified type of grouped data frames).

title: Implement native shaped assignment
description:
This PR implements native assignment for arrays through `vec_assign()`.

It also refactors some of the existing tooling in `slice-array.R` and extracts out common pieces into `strides.h`.

I have also figured out how to more efficiently slice arrays, so I've made some major improvements to `vec_slice()`. `vec_assign()` uses the more efficient method as well.

The way this generally works is that we fix the "shape" dimensions and then step along the size dimension using simple addition to either slice or assign everything required for that fixed shape. Then we increment the shape and repeat until we run out of shape dimensions.

So for `vec_slice(<array[3, 2, 3]>, c(1, 3))` we would:

- Start at `[X, 1, 1]`
- Then jump to `[1, 1, 1]`
- Then jump to `[3, 1, 1]`
- Then increment the shape to `[X, 2, 1]`
- And repeat until we hit `[X, 2, 3]`



Slicing and assignment are now quite fast!

`vec_assign()` has more overhead than `vec_slice()` right now, because it uses `vec_coercible_cast(value, x)`, which has to call back to R for `vec_ptype2()` and `vec_cast()` methods for shaped inputs.

``` r
library(vctrs)

x <- matrix(1:500000 + 0L, nrow = 10000)
idx <- 5001:10000 + 0L
x_value <- vec_slice(x, idx)

bench::mark(
  vec_slice(x, idx),
  x[idx,],
  iterations = 2000
)
# Master
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression             min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>        <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_slice(x, idx)    281µs    408µs     2435.     977KB     45.9
#> 2 x[idx, ]             307µs    383µs     2519.     977KB     48.5

# This PR
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression             min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>        <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_slice(x, idx)    153µs    248µs     3964.    1003KB     75.5
#> 2 x[idx, ]             307µs    436µs     2377.     977KB     44.8

bench::mark(
  vec_assign(x, idx, x_value),
  `[<-`(x, idx, , x_value),
  iterations = 10000
)
# Master
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression                       min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>                  <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_assign(x, idx, x_value)   1.02ms   1.41ms      696.     5.1MB     52.5
#> 2 `[<-`(x, idx, , x_value)    342.77µs 503.61µs     1968.    1.91MB     85.2

# This PR
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression                       min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>                  <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_assign(x, idx, x_value)    427µs    572µs     1674.    2.11MB     69.7
#> 2 `[<-`(x, idx, , x_value)       326µs    511µs     1917.    1.91MB    124.
```

With a larger dimensionality, the difference is even more pronounced

```r
y <- array(1:500000 + 0L, dim = c(1000, 10, 50))
idx <- 1:1000 + 0L
y_value <- vec_slice(y, idx)

bench::mark(
  vec_slice(y, idx),
  y[idx,,],
  iterations = 1000
)
# Master
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression             min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>        <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_slice(y, idx) 736.79µs 922.66µs     1050.    1.91MB     46.5
#> 2 y[idx, , ]          1.69ms   1.92ms      510.    1.91MB     22.3

# This PR
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression             min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>        <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_slice(y, idx) 286.52µs  416.7µs     2376.    1.91MB    103. 
#> 2 y[idx, , ]          1.65ms    1.9ms      517.    1.91MB     21.5

bench::mark(
  vec_assign(y, idx, y_value),
  `[<-`(y, idx, , , y_value),
  iterations = 5000
)
# Master
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression                       min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>                  <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_assign(y, idx, y_value)   2.79ms   3.88ms      256.    5.74MB     20.5
#> 2 `[<-`(y, idx, , , y_value)    1.72ms   2.06ms      478.    1.91MB     16.4

# This PR
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression                       min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>                  <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_assign(y, idx, y_value)  646.7µs 820.89µs     1197.    1.91MB     56.4
#> 2 `[<-`(y, idx, , , y_value)    1.72ms   2.16ms      465.    1.91MB     30.3
```


should this not have been an error? You can cast from, for example, `<double>` to `<foobar>` without writing a method for it? I found this super confusing when writing an S4 `bdays` class that "contained" an integer, and then was automatically able to do:

Closes #952

title: Double dispatch manually in `vec_ptype2()`
description:
We look up the left ptype2 method in the vctrs method table, then we look up the right method in the method table of the environment of the left method. This way the process for implementing methods mostly stays the same and we continue to benefit from registration via roxygen2 and R CMD check support. However implementation is now simplified:

* No longer need to worry about order of dispatch, a simple `UseMethod("vec_ptype2.class")` is sufficient.

* No longer need to implement default methods.

In a future PR, it will be easy to disable inheritance in ptype2 dispatch and avoid the ambiguities it causes.

I struggled for a while with an infloop involving partial frames and unimplemented ptype2 methods. I understand the infloop (ptype2-default calls ptype2 again for partial objects) but not how it worked before. Not sure how to solve it, so I just disabled the implicated test. Since partial types are not very useful right now, we can revisit these later.

The `AsIs` class was a bit problematic because it relies on a default ptype2 method. We'll probably want to remove support for those, but this will need to wait until vctrs supports native wrapper types.

I'll update the docs and vignette after the inheritance PR. Launching revdeps now so we monitor the backward compatibility of these important changes.

title: Implement `vec_rep()` and `vec_rep_each()`
description:
Closes #496 
Closes #860 

This PR implements `vec_rep()` and `vec_rep_each()` and soft-deprecates `vec_repeat()`.

It is not as fast as the custom implementation I had created for dplyr, as that wasn't generic and was just for integer vectors https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/496#issuecomment-590466282.

This solution takes the same approach as `vec_repeat()`, building an index vector and then calling `vec_slice()`. While we could get substantial performance improvements by trying to imitate what is done in https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/496#issuecomment-590466282, I think it is too much work, since we'd essentially have to handle all of the fallback edge cases that `vec_slice_impl()` does. If we think it is worth it to go that route though, I can give it a shot.

``` r
library(vctrs)

set.seed(123)

x <- 1:5000 + 0
times <- sample(1e2, 5000, replace = TRUE)

bench::mark(
  rep(x, times),
  vec_rep_each(x, times),
  iterations = 10000
)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression                  min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>             <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 rep(x, times)             354µs    535µs     1819.    1.93MB     69.9
#> 2 vec_rep_each(x, times)    273µs    450µs     2258.    2.91MB    166.

bench::mark(
  rep(x, each = 1000),
  vec_rep_each(x, 1000),
  vec_repeat(x, each = 1000),
  iterations = 50
)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 6
#>   expression                      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>                 <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 rep(x, each = 1000)         65.51ms  67.73ms      14.6    38.1MB     6.24
#> 2 vec_rep_each(x, 1000)        6.87ms   7.67ms     129.     57.2MB   210.  
#> 3 vec_repeat(x, each = 1000)  96.03ms  97.97ms      10.1    57.3MB    16.5

bench::mark(
  rep(x, 1000),
  vec_rep(x, 1000),
  vec_repeat(x, times = 1000),
  iterations = 100
)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 6
#>   expression                       min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>                  <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 rep(x, 1000)                   6.3ms   7.36ms     137.     38.1MB     48.1
#> 2 vec_rep(x, 1000)              7.43ms   7.92ms     125.     57.2MB    187. 
#> 3 vec_repeat(x, times = 1000)  30.93ms  33.06ms      29.3    57.2MB     47.8
```

title: Remove default args
description:
I think the default `arg` values end up to be misleading for end users because they refer to internal details of internal functions.

This brings up the issue of how to refer to arguments in error messages. `vec_recycle()` now uses the same approach as in subscript errors and uses a general noun "Input".

Before:

```r
#> Error: `x` can't be recycled to size 4.
```

After:

```r
#> Error: Input can't be recycled to size 4.
```

If `arg = "foo"` is supplied, this is:

```r
#> Error: Input `foo` can't be recycled to size 4.
```

We should standardise on a user-friendly noun for referring to arguments. I thought "Input" is shorter and less jargony than "Argument".

title: Add `vec_ptype2()` and `vec_cast()` methods for table objects
description:
Closes #904 
Closes tidyverse/dplyr#4963

This roughly follows how ptype2 and cast methods have been implemented for glue. 
https://github.com/tidyverse/glue/blob/master/R/vctrs.R

The example from tidyverse/dplyr#4963:

``` r
library(dplyr)

ex <- table(iris$Species) %>%
  expand.grid() 

ex
#>   Var1
#> 1   50
#> 2   50
#> 3   50

class(ex$Var1)
#> [1] "table"

ex <- mutate(ex, Var2 = Var1)

ex
#>   Var1 Var2
#> 1   50   50
#> 2   50   50
#> 3   50   50

class(ex$Var2)
#> [1] "table"
```

<sup>Created on 2020-03-11 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

We do have at least one weird edge case. With `vec_rbind()`, we call `as_df_row()` on each input. For array-like objects with a dimensionality of 2, this calls `as.data.frame()`. But there is an `as.data.frame.table()` method that does something different from what it does for arrays. It doesn't error, it's just odd and incorrect, but I think `vec_rbind()` will have to be tweaked in a separate PR to fix it.

``` r
library(vctrs)

x <- vctrs:::new_table(1:4, c(2L, 2L))
dimnames(x) <- list(c("r1", "r2"), c("c1", "c2"))

x
#>    c1 c2
#> r1  1  3
#> r2  2  4

as.data.frame(x)
#>   Var1 Var2 Freq
#> 1   r1   c1    1
#> 2   r2   c1    2
#> 3   r1   c2    3
#> 4   r2   c2    4

vec_rbind(x, x)
#>   c1 c2 NA
#> 1 r1 c1  1
#> 2 r2 c1  2
#> 3 r1 c2  3
#> 4 r2 c2  4
#> 5 r1 c1  1
#> 6 r2 c1  2
#> 7 r1 c2  3
#> 8 r2 c2  4
```

title: Improve support of foreign classes
description:
In combining operations `vec_c()`, `vec_rbind()`, `vec_unchop()`, for homogeneously classed inputs. Closes #776.

* Like before, `c()` is used as fallback. However we check in advance for a `c()` implementation. If not found, we use the second fallback.

* Like `vec_ptype2()`, `vec_cast()` now uses `is_same_type()`. If the types are the same (their prototypes all have the same attributes), we no-op. Combining operations restore the attributes after concatenation.

I don't remember why I didn't implement this fallback immediately, I think it had to do with issues caused by method inheritance and `vctrs_vctr` inheriting from the base type, which we have since disabled.

Currently `vec_rbind()` doesn't fall back to `c()`, I'll implement this separately. Also still need to provide hints about implementing vctrs methods for incompatible homogeneously classed inputs (see #922).

title: Fix `vec_unchop()` fallback with repeated assignment
description:
The rare case of `vec_unchop()` having to fall back + having repeated assignment in the `indices` was broken. This fixes that. It uses the flattened `indices` vector to build a `locations` vector that will be used to slice the result of the `vec_c_fallback()`. It builds the `locations` vector in such a way that:

- Locations that are never touched are sliced with `NA_integer_`

- Indices that are repeated use the value of the last one

(This is identical to what the non-fallback does)

``` r
library(vctrs)

x <- c("a", "b")
y <- "c"

x_foo <- structure(x, class = "vctrs_foobar")
y_foo <- structure(y, class = "vctrs_foobar")

c.vctrs_foobar <- function(...) {
  dots <- list(...)
  dots <- lapply(dots, unclass)
  out <- do.call(c, dots)
  structure(out, class = "vctrs_foobar")
}
```

```r
# Master

vec_unchop(list(x, y), list(c(1, 2), 1))
#> [1] "c" "b" NA

vec_unchop(list(x_foo, y_foo), list(c(1, 2), 1))
#> [1] "a" "c" "b"
#> attr(,"class")
#> [1] "vctrs_foobar"
```

```r
# This PR

vec_unchop(list(x, y), list(c(1, 2), 1))
#> [1] "c" "b" NA

vec_unchop(list(x_foo, y_foo), list(c(1, 2), 1))
#> [1] "c" "b" NA 
#> attr(,"class")
#> [1] "vctrs_foobar"
```

title: Implement `list_sizes()`
description:
`vec_sizes()` is to `vec_size()` what `lengths()` is to `length()`: 

``` r
library(vctrs)

data <- list(iris, mtcars, 1:10)
vec_sizes(data)
#> [1] 150  32  10
```

The 😈 plan is to use this in a vctrs based implementation of things like `dplyr::summarise()` and `dplyr::mutate()` e.g. evaluate the expression in each group and then assert that the sizes are good (all equal to 1 if summaries, equal to the group sizes on a mutate). 

The PR is wip, if we want that I'll add unit tests, etc ...

title: Attempt to lookup S4 `c()` methods in `vec_c()`
description:
Closes #919 
Closes tidyverse/dplyr#4986
Related to https://github.com/tidyverse/lubridate/issues/721

This PR adds a way to check for S4 `c()` methods to fall back to in `vec_c()`. The implementation is derived from looking at `methods:::.showMethodsTable()`. S4 generic functions have an environment attached to them, and that environment contains another environment, `.MTable`, which is the methods table for that specific generic. That can be used to check if a method exists or not.

``` r
library(vctrs)
library(lubridate, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

vec_c(days(1:2), 3)
#> Error: No common type for `..1` <Period> and `..2` <double>.

vec_c(days(1:2), days(3))
#> [1] "1d 0H 0M 0S" "2d 0H 0M 0S" "3d 0H 0M 0S"
```

It seems to also work even if you don't explicitly load lubridate, which is nice

```r
library(vctrs)

vec_c(lubridate::days(1:2), lubridate::days(3))
#> [1] "1d 0H 0M 0S" "2d 0H 0M 0S" "3d 0H 0M 0S"
```

title: Fix indirections in child errors
description:
Closes tidyverse/tibble#735.

@krlmlr This had to do with closure-inlined `cnd_body()` methods and child errors. The fix was rather tricky, but I think these rules might offer a general solution:

```
* Close over the parent when a child error is created outside of a
  given error class. For instance lossy cast errors need to consistently
  refer to their actual error object.

* Conversely, don't close over the parent when a child error is
  created within a given class. This allows subscript errors to pick up
  updated `subscript_arg` fields.
```

description:
This PR further optimizes `vec_group_loc()`, which should directly result in performance improvements for `group_by()`.

In Instruments I noticed that the biggest killer in `vec_group_loc()` is the double deference in a tight loop of `INTEGER(VECTOR_ELT())`. That can be replaced with an array of integer pointers that index directly into those integer vectors. That really helped.

Side note: It is insane how fast this is if you order the data ahead of time. As pointed out by @brodieG

```r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(vctrs)

set.seed(42)

g <- sample(1e6, 1e7, replace = TRUE)
tbl <- tibble(g = g)

o <- order(g)
ordered_tbl <- tbl[o,]
```

title: Add support for AsIs
description:
Closes #906 

This PR adds support for AsIs. Since it is like a parameterized type, the class is always retained when it is involved in type2 coercion.

- New `vec_ptype2.AsIs()` which strips the AsIs class, finds the common type by re-calling `vec_ptype2()`, and then adds it back

- New `vec_cast.AsIs()` which strips the AsIs class, casts, and then adds it back if `to` was AsIs

- `vec_default_cast()` and `vec_default_ptype2()` have been tweaked to know about AsIs, and work like the new methods. They strip the class, find the common type, and add it back if required. This makes things like `vec_ptype2("x", I("y"))` work without the need for the extra method.

A few examples:

``` r
library(vctrs)

x <- I(1L)
y <- I(1)

# AsIs<int> with AsIs<int> = AsIs<int>
vec_ptype2(x, x)
#> integer(0)
class(vec_ptype2(x, x))
#> [1] "AsIs"

# AsIs<int> with AsIs<dbl> = AsIs<dbl>
vec_ptype2(x, y)
#> numeric(0)
class(vec_ptype2(x, y))
#> [1] "AsIs"

# AsIs<int> with <dbl> = AsIs<dbl>
vec_ptype2(x, 1)
#> numeric(0)
class(vec_ptype2(x, 1))
#> [1] "AsIs"

# Carries through to vec_c()
vec_c(x, 1)
#> [1] 1 1
typeof(vec_c(x, 1))
#> [1] "double"
class(vec_c(x, 1))
#> [1] "AsIs"
```

Notably, R retains the AsIs class when slicing, but not when using `c()`. If we need to mock this behavior to get dplyr revdeps to work, I can adjust this PR to do so.

``` r
library(vctrs)

x <- I(1L)

x[c(1, 1)]
#> [1] 1 1
class(x[c(1, 1)])
#> [1] "AsIs"

c(x, x)
#> [1] 1 1
class(c(x, x))
#> [1] "integer"

c(x, 1)
#> [1] 1 1
class(c(x, 1))
#> [1] "numeric"
```

title: Use POSIXct for POSIXlt's comparison and equality proxy
description:
I am now convinced that we should just convert a POSIXlt object to POSIXct to get its comparison and equality proxy. It is too messy otherwise, with too many edge cases.

For the comparison proxy, we currently have a bug with DST because the comparison proxy doesn't include the `dst` field. But we can't just include that field because it won't be `NA` when the rest of the fields (like year, mon, etc) are `NA`, which would break `vec_equal_na()`.

I think the easiest way to do this is to just convert to POSIXct.

We will need to do this for the equality proxy as well, otherwise `vec_complete_cases()` won't work correctly. Currently the equality proxy for POSIXlt falls back to `vec_proxy()` which creates a data frame out of the entire record structure. This is a problem for `vec_complete_cases()` because the `gmtoffset` field can be `NA` if the offset is just "unknown" even if there is actual data for that element ([here](https://bugs.r-project.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=16648) is an example), so it incorrectly will return `FALSE`. Again, converting to POSIXct removes this problem.

``` r
library(vctrs)

# 1am in EDT
x <- as.POSIXlt("2020-11-01 01:00:00", tz = "America/New_York")

# "falls back" to 1am again, but in EST
y <- as.POSIXlt(x + 3600)

x
#> [1] "2020-11-01 01:00:00 EDT"
y
#> [1] "2020-11-01 01:00:00 EST"

# look the same, but they are not!
vec_proxy_compare(x)
#>   year mon mday hour min sec
#> 1  120  10    1    1   0   0
vec_proxy_compare(y)
#>   year mon mday hour min sec
#> 1  120  10    1    1   0   0

# wrong!
vec_order(c(x, y))
#> [1] 1 2
vec_order(c(y, x))
#> [1] 1 2

order(c(x, y))
#> [1] 1 2
order(c(y, x))
#> [1] 2 1

x_ct <- as.POSIXct(x)
y_ct <- as.POSIXct(y)

# correct!
vec_order(c(x_ct, y_ct))
#> [1] 1 2
vec_order(c(y_ct, x_ct))
#> [1] 2 1
```

title: Add `vec_proxy()` and `vec_restore()` methods for factors
description:
Closes #705 

This PR implements `vec_proxy()` and `vec_restore()` methods for factors and ordered factors.

- `vec_proxy()` methods are trivial, and just exist to make `vec_slice()` not fallback to `[.factor`.

- `vec_restore()` methods do a few checks before handing off to `vec_restore_default()`

   - The main check is to ensure that the number of levels implied by the integer vector `x` aligns with the number of levels in the factor `to`. @lionel- had the idea to just check the maximum value of `x` against the length of the levels of `to`. `NA` values get ignored for this check.

   - I've intercepted the C level `vec_restore()` to hand off to `vec_restore_bare_factor()` directly to avoid R level dispatch.

I think if we wanted to we could also intercept `vec_proxy_method()` in some way for these known cases so we don't have to look to R to find the `vec_proxy.factor()` method.

Performance is a _little_ better for slicing, but I wasn't expecting much here.

``` r
library(vctrs)
set.seed(123)

x <- factor("x")

bench::mark(
  vec_slice(x, 1L),
  x[1L],
  iterations = 100000
)
```

title: Add `na_equal` parameter to `vec_match()`
description:
Closes #718.

* Support propagation of `NA` in hashing functions. Elements with `NA` are hashed with the constant `HASH_MISSING`, hard-coded to 1. This way we can avoid missingness comparisons when they are not needed.

* Dictionary structure gains a `equal_missing()` method to compare elements to the missing value.

* New `na_equal` parameter for dictionary initialisation. When `false`, the dicitionary vector is hashed with `HASH_MISSING` support.

* New `dict_is_missing()` function to check whether an element of a dictionary is missing.

* `vec_equal()` now uses these features to implement `na_equal = FALSE`.

One question is whether `NA` should propagate across columns when matching data frames. The alternative is to consider that only rows full of `NA`s are missing. It seems it's more consistent and useful to propagate across columns, which is implemented here:

```r
df <- data_frame(x = 1, y = NA, z = 2)

vec_match(df, df)
#> [1] 1

vec_match(df, df, na_equal = FALSE)
#> [1] NA
```

title: Restrict `vec_unchop()` and `vec_chop()` to positive integer locations
description:
Closes #846 

As discussed at https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/pull/834#issuecomment-589435201, since `vec_unchop()`'s `indices` argument is all about placing elements of `x` in specified _locations_, it doesn't make sense to allow character/logical subscripts in that function. To align `vec_chop()` with `vec_unchop()`, I've restricted `vec_chop()` to only allow positive integer locations as well. `vec_unchop()` could technically allow character and logical, but it doesn't feel useful.

`NA_integer_` is still a valid location.

In the next PR I will rename `indices` to `locations`

title: Move fallback handling into `vec_assign_impl()`
description:
Closes #853 
Closes #625 
Closes tidyverse/tidyr#788
Solves (partially) DavisVaughan/slider#2, will be completely solved with additional slider work on my end

This PR moves the fallback handling of `vec_assign()` into `vec_assign_impl()`. The separation is:

-  The caller of `vec_assign_impl()` handles
   - Coercible casting of `value`. If you already know the type is correct you don't have to cast.
   - Recycling `value`. Same reasoning as above.
   - Proxying and restoring the output container, so it is only done once. (Useful for things like `vec_c()`)

- `vec_assign_impl()` handles:
   - proxy-ing `value`. Required to be able to fallback using the non-proxied `value`
   - Handling fallback behavior

This PR also fixes a few bugs that came up with the awful corrupt objects that are `OBJECT()`s but don't have a class.

The one drawback here is that `vec_assign()` now calls `vec_recycle()` on the un-proxied `value`, then hands off to `vec_assign_impl()`, which proxies and might allocate. This is slightly less efficient than proxying first, then recycling, but I can live with this tradeoff to have a clear separation of responsibility.

The other change here is that we now `vec_restore()` after calling the fallback to `[<-`. I feel like this is the correct thing to do, and probably won't hurt, but it did require a tweak to a test that "expected" the object to not be restored.

title: Cache vector types and pointers in dictionaries
description:
Branched from #847. 

This caches the `enum vctrs_type`, the array pointers, and the comparison operation (as in Davis' experiment https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/compare/master...DavisVaughan:type-remember) in the dictionaries. This avoids the need for dereferencing the `SEXP` multiple times when comparing elements for equality.

For data frames we store an array of types and pointers, one for each column. I also tried caching a slice of the data frame in row-major order to improve locality when many comparisons are required. This improved performance in specific cases but was disappointing overall.

```r
## 200 uniques
## Number of comparisons: 999800
## Number of collisions: 0
x <- sample(1:1e2, 1e6, TRUE) + 0L
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = rep(1:2, length.out = length(x)))
bench::mark(
  uloc = vec_unique_loc(df$x),
  df_uloc = vec_unique_loc(df),
  check = FALSE,
  iterations = 100
)[1:8]

#> # master
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` n_itr  n_gc
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl> <int> <dbl>
#> 1 uloc         10.3ms   11.4ms      85.2    11.8MB    10.5     89    11
#> 2 df_uloc      66.8ms   68.7ms      14.4    11.8MB     1.78    89    11

#> # perf-dict-mem
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` n_itr  n_gc
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl> <int> <dbl>
#> 1 uloc         4.72ms   5.08ms     188.     11.8MB    125.     60    40
#> 2 df_uloc     16.08ms  17.08ms      58.2    11.8MB     28.7    67    33


## Many columns - 200 uniques
x <- sample(1:1e2, 1e6, TRUE) + 0L
df <- data.frame(
  x = x,
  y = rep(1:2, length.out = length(x)),
  z1 = duplicate(x),
  z2 = duplicate(x),
  z3 = duplicate(x),
  z4 = duplicate(x)
)
bench::mark(
  uloc = vec_unique_loc(df$x),
  df_uloc = vec_unique_loc(df),
```

title: Add support for `numeric_version`
description:
Part of #723

This is an interesting type because `c()` and `[` wrap vectors of size > 1 in a list-of-like type. To support those natively in vctrs, we'd need some way of customising the "wrapper" type of atomic classes.

I haven't implemented `vec_ptype2()` with character because it's unclear what is the richer type in this case [^1]. To reproduce base R semantics, it'd have to be numeric-version. Do we consider that numeric-version is a restriction on strings? Another class representing restricted strings is factor, for which character is considered to be richer:

```r
vec_ptype2(factor("foo"), "bar")
#> character(0)
```

Perhaps we need to distinguish between hard restrictions (like `list_of`) and soft restrictions (like `factor`). Choosing one or the other is a matter of balancing safety (programming) and friction (interactivity). Since numeric-version is mostly used for programming, safety seems to have greater weight.

But then, does ptype2 really always return the "richer" type? I think this touches the issue of richer behaviour (e.g. restrictions) versus richer data coverage. This is currently a weakness in our theory. Perhaps soft restrictions are not behaviour, but hard restrictions are.

[^1]: And also we'd need to implement proxy/restore and deal with the issue of wrapper type mentioned above.

title: Explicitly export symbols
description:
Fixes #862.
Supersedes #863.

This makes it possible to link to `vctrs.so` without symbol conflicts. To enable explicit exporting outside the R build system, set `CFLAGS` to

```
-fvisibility=hidden -DHAVE_VISIBILITY_ATTRIBUTE
```

The `Makevars` file also sets `$(C_VISIBILITY)`. By default this disables exporting of symbols on platform that support it. MacOS does not support it but Linux platforms (used in CI) do. By setting `C_VISIBILITY`, we ensure our package remains compatible with `-fvisibility=hidden`.

Compatibility with hidden visibility is very easy to achieve for R package that use symbol registration (which is now enforced by CRAN). The only native symbol to export is `R_init_*packagename*` (it must be discoverable by R to register the function pointers exported with the R mechanism). Rcpp projects do not need to do anything because the init function is tagged with `RcppExport` which sets the visibility attribute: https://github.com/RcppCore/Rcpp/blob/master/inst/include/RcppCommon.h#L139

title: Implement `vec_is_coercible()` in C
description:
Adds `r_try_catch()` to the internal API. It is inspired by the R API function `R_tryCatch()` and has the advantage of being available in all R versions with the same implementation (`R_tryCatch()` is buggy or non-available in older Rs).

```c
ERR r_try_catch(void (*fn)(void*),
                void* fn_data,
                SEXP cnd_sym,
                void (*hnd)(void*),
                void* hnd_data);
```

* It takes callbacks and data for the normal and catch case, and a symbol of the handled condition class.

* It returns `ERR`, which is a simple alias to `SEXP`. The goal of this alias is to indicate a NULL-able `SEXP`. The C NULL is easier to work with for error handling and is made use of in an upcoming PR.

`vec_is_coercible()` is implemented with `r_try_catch()` and now available in the C API as well. Its performance is slightly improved in the normal path:

```r
bench::mark(
```
