title: Fix data frame & proxied object name handling in `vec_c()`
description:
Closes #524 
Closes #520 

This PR:

- Implements `vec_set_names()`. It has the following semantics:
   - Never sets row names on data frames
   - Sets names on unclassed vectors
   - Sets row names on unclassed matrices/arrays
   - Falls back to `names<-` on classed vectors
   - Falls back to `rownames<-` on classed matrices/arrays
- Uses `vec_set_names()` in `vec_c()` for better name handling with proxied objects
- Tweaks `has_names` in `vec_c()` to completely avoid outer name handling when the `ptype` is a data frame. Outer names are completely ignored here.

Here are a few examples of what this fixes:

``` r
library(vctrs)
library(rlang)
```

```r
# before
vec_c(x = data.frame(xx = 1), y = data.frame(yy = 2))
#>    x  y
#> 1  1 NA
#> 2 NA  2

# after
vec_c(x = data.frame(xx = 1), y = data.frame(yy = 2))
#>   xx yy
#> 1  1 NA
#> 2 NA  2
```

```r
# before
vec_c(x = data.frame(xx = 1), y = data.frame(xx = 2))
#> Error in vec_c(x = data.frame(xx = 1), y = data.frame(xx = 2)): 'names' attribute [2] must be the same length as the vector [1]

# after
vec_c(x = data.frame(xx = 1), y = data.frame(xx = 2))
#>   xx
#> 1  1
#> 2  2
```

```r
datetime_lt <- as.POSIXlt(new_datetime(0))
datetimes_lt <- as.POSIXlt(new_datetime(c(0, 1)))
named_datetime_lt <- set_names(datetime_lt, "dt_name")
```

```r
# before
vec_c(x = datetime_lt)
#> [1] "1969-12-31 19:00:00 EST"

# after
vec_c(x = datetime_lt)
#>                         x 
#> "1969-12-31 19:00:00 EST"
```

```r
# before
vec_c(x = datetimes_lt, .name_spec = "{outer}_{inner}")
#> [1] "1969-12-31 19:00:00 EST" "1969-12-31 19:00:01 EST"

# after
vec_c(x = datetimes_lt, .name_spec = "{outer}_{inner}")
#>                       x_1                       x_2 
#> "1969-12-31 19:00:00 EST" "1969-12-31 19:00:01 EST"
```

```r
# before
vec_c(x = named_datetime_lt, .name_spec = "{outer}_{inner}")
#> [1] "1969-12-31 19:00:00 EST"

# after
vec_c(x = named_datetime_lt, .name_spec = "{outer}_{inner}")
#>                 x_dt_name 
#> "1969-12-31 19:00:00 EST"
```

title: Teach `vec_slice_impl()` about `compact_seq()` + implement decreasing `compact_seq()`s
description:
Closes #490 
Closes #489 

This PR does two things:

- It teaches `vec_slice_impl()` how to work with `compact_seq()` objects
- It allows `compact_seq()`s to be negative by redefining a `compact_seq()` object in terms of a start location, a total size, and a step size (`+/-1`). Both `vec_slice_impl()` and `vec_assign_impl()` know how to deal with this.

We don't have a use case for this in vctrs, but I do have a potential use case for this in a C impl of `slide()` so I figured I would add it. 

I have exposed `vec_slice_seq()` to the R side for testing purposes.

Notes: 

- `compact_seq()`s are now _inclusive_ on both endpoints: `[from, to]` rather than the previous behavior of `[from, to)`. The original behavior was a bit hard to reason about with decreasing sequences, and kept you from being able to compute a decreasing sequence with only the 1st value, i.e. you would try `[0, 0)` but the size of the sequence would be computed as 0 and the sequence would be empty. Now it would be computed as `[0, 0]`, which is a sequence of 1 value at position 1.

- You can't have a seq with `NA` in it, so you'll see that `NA_VALUE` is not passed through in the macros.

- The use of `memcpy()` in `ASSIGN_COMPACT` was replaced with an assignment loop to be compatible with decreasing compact sequences. A few bench marks didn't show any loss in performance.

Using `compact_seq()`s in `vec_slice_impl()` can have some nice performance improvements:

``` r
library(nycflights13)
library(vctrs)

x <- flights

nrow(x)
#> [1] 336776

vec_slice_seq <- vctrs:::vec_slice_seq

bench::mark(
  vec_slice_seq(x, 0L, 99999L),
  vec_slice(x, 1:100000),
  x[1:100000,],
  iterations = 1000
)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 6
#>   expression                       min  median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>                   <bch:t> <bch:t>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
```

title: Export `vec_split_id()`
description:
Closes #514 
CC @romainfrancois 

- Renames `vec_duplicate_split()` as `vec_split_id()` and exports it
- `vec_split_id()` returns a data frame of the:
   - `key`: Unique values in `x`
   - `id`: A list of integers containing the positions of the keys in `x`
- `vec_split()` was updated to reflect the new api.

Questions:

- Should the `id` column be a `list_of<int()>`? We don't have a way to do this from the C side, so it would have to happen on the R side. As long as it doesn't affect performance much, it might make sense.
- Does using `out$id <- NULL` in `vec_split()` look okay? An alternative is creating a completely new data frame with `new_data_frame(list(key = out$key, val = vals))`, but I think it is slightly slower.

title: Convert `as_df_row()` inputs to lists with elements of size 1
description:
Closes #480 

This PR technically fixes #480, but I am hoping it can be improved, as I think it will be a bit slow in the long run.

It replaces the call to `r_as_list()` with an alternative, `as_list_row()`, that does something slightly different. It turns its input into a list such that each element of the result is of size 1. Meaning that `list(1:2, 1)` becomes `list(list(1:2), list(1))`. Another way to think of it is that it iterates through `x`, calling `vec_slice(x, i)` for each `i`, and places the result of the slice into the `i`th element of the output list. I think this is the most consistent way for `as_df_row()` to work.

I think `as_list_row()` is going to be somewhat slow though, as the repeated calls to `vec_slice()` might be a problem. Note that this isn't called for data frames (`as_df_row_impl()` early exits), but is called when the user does something like `vec_rbind(1:5)`, which might hurt performance. I'm open to other ideas!

title: Teach `vec_slice()` about `compact_seq()`
description:

Closes #489 

This PR teaches `vec_slice_impl()` how to work with `compact_seq()` objects.

title: Fix performance of data frames containing objects
description:
- Take equality proxy recursively before making equality comparisons. This way we only dispatch once on `vec_proxy()`, instead of once per comparison. Closes #498.

- Dictionaries must now be protected because they contain the proxied data as reference. The patch removes `dict_free()` and introduces `PROTECT_DICT()` to make the semantics clearer. The former makes it seem like dictionaries can be freed at any point in the lifetime of the program. For compatibility with rchk, `PROTECT_DICT()` is a macro that takes a protection counter. `UNPROTECT()` can then be called the normal way.

title: Fix hash test results on big-endian systems.
description:
The result is the same, but looking at the *raw* bytes, the results are
byte swapped. So comparing against a list of bytes from a little-endian
system won't work.

Just swap the byte order before comparing against the ground truth
values. This means there's no need to save two copies of the ground
truth.

Fixes #492.

title: Implement `compact_rep()`
description:
Closes #472 

This PR introduces `compact_rep()`. It is similar to `compact_seq()`, but takes a single value `i` and repeats it `n` times.

**With this PR we gain performance at the cost of more C defines**

`vec_slice()` has been made aware of `compact_rep` objects, and `vec_recycle()` and the C level `vec_init()` use it.

Because `vec_init()` and `vec_recycle()` are used in `vec_c()`, `vec_rbind()`, and `vec_cbind()`, these all inherit a little bit of the performance.

_It would be great if the R level `vec_init()` used the C level version of `vec_init()` so it could get these benefits too._

title: used `vec_size()` instead of `Rf_length()` in `vec_dim()` (pillar #167)
description:
This PR is related to my issue about `list_of()` size display in the list-columns (now transferred to https://github.com/r-lib/pillar/issues/167). After digging into the source code, I think this issue lies in the **vctrs**, not **pillar**. For robustness, `Rf_length()` is replaced by `vec_size()` in `vec_dim()`. It fixes the size issue.

``` r
library(vctrs)

new_rational <- function(n = integer(), d = integer()) {
  vec_assert(n, ptype = integer())
  vec_assert(d, ptype = integer())
  
  new_rcrd(list(n = n, d = d), class = "vctrs_rational")
}

rational <- function(n, d) {
  c(n, d) %<-% vec_cast_common(n, d, .to = integer())
  c(n, d) %<-% vec_recycle_common(n, d)
  
  new_rational(n, d)
}

format.vctrs_rational <- function(x, ...) {
  n <- field(x, "n")
  d <- field(x, "d")
  
  out <- paste0(n, "/", d)
  out[is.na(n) | is.na(d)] <- NA
  
  out
}

vec_ptype_abbr.vctrs_rational <- function(x, ...) "rtnl"
vec_ptype_full.vctrs_rational <- function(x, ...) "rational"

x <- rational(1, 1:10)
x
#> <rational[10]>
#>  [1] 1/1  1/2  1/3  1/4  1/5  1/6  1/7  1/8  1/9  1/10

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
iris %>% 
  group_by(Species) %>% 
  summarise(
    ratio = list_of(rational(as.integer(Sepal.Length), as.integer(Sepal.Width)))
  )
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   Species           ratio
#>   <fct>      <list<rtnl>>
#> 1 setosa             [50]
#> 2 versicolor         [50]
#> 3 virginica          [50]
```

title: Use 0-size tidyverse recycling rules consistently
description:
Closes #299 

These changes to `vec_size2()` and `shape_broadcast()` enforce correct tidyverse recycling rules when comparing length-0 dimensions (those laid out in https://github.com/tidyverse/principles/issues/13#issuecomment-500996394).

Specifically, the common length of `0` and `2` is now an error. 

``` r
x  <- array(1, c(1, 2))
to <- array(1, c(1, 0))
vctrs:::shape_common(x, to)
#> Incompatible lengths: 2, 0.
```

The common length of `0` and `1` is `0`, as it was before.

``` r
x  <- array(1, c(1, 1))
to <- array(1, c(1, 0))
vctrs:::shape_common(x, to)
#> [1] 0
```

When broadcasting _to_ a shape, the dimensions you are broadcasting to must be exactly the same, unless the dimension you are broadcasting from is `1`, in which case that can be broadcast to anything. All but the last of these examples produce the same result as before this PR, but I present them as a group to make the argument (the last one previously allowed you to broadcast from `2` down to `0`)

``` r
# 1 can be broadcast _to_ anything
x  <- array(1, c(1, 1))
to <- array(1, c(1, 0))
vctrs:::shape_broadcast(x, to)
#>     
#> [1,]

to <- array(1, c(1, 2))
vctrs:::shape_broadcast(x, to)
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    1    1
```

``` r
# everything else must be broadcast
# to the _exact_ same dimensions to be allowed

# 0 cannot be broadcast to 1
x  <- array(1, c(1, 0))
to <- array(1, c(1, 1))
vctrs:::shape_broadcast(x, to)
#> Can't cast <double[,0]> to <double[,1]>
#> Non-recyclable dimensions

# 2 cannot be broadcast to 0
x  <- array(1, c(1, 2))
to <- array(1, c(1, 0))
vctrs:::shape_broadcast(x, to)
#> Can't cast <double[,2]> to <double[,0]>
#> Non-recyclable dimensions
```

I think the only thing you might have a question about is the fact that this means you can't broadcast from 2 down to 0. You can currently do this with `vec_recycle()`.

``` r
vctrs::vec_recycle(1:2, 0)
#> integer(0)
```

It also occurred to me while thinking about this that there are really two types of recycling rules. One set for determining a common length. And one set for determining if you can actually recycle from length X to length Y. The result of the first set of rules is guaranteed to be an allowed length in the second set of rules. The current impl of `vec_recycle()` implies that the second set of rules might be more flexible though, allowing that you can recycle from `2` down to `0`, where the first set of rules would have never generated `0` as the common length of `2` and something else.

title: Export `vec_default_type2()` to reduce boilerplate
description:
Closes #380.

* The logical method of `vec_type2()` now returns the type of `y` when `x` is unspecified.

* Other `vec_type2()` methods for base types now call `vec_default_type2()`. If `y` is unspecified, the type of `x` is returned.

* Because of this some additional boilerplate is necessary for `list` because the common type is how we prevent `list[1] <- NA` from working (it should be `list[[1]] <- NA` or `list[1] <- list(NA)`).

* `vec_default_type2()` is now exported.

* If the default type2 method of a class calls `vec_default_type2()`, it is no longer necessary to define unspecified methods. Documentation in the vignette is updated.

title: Improve `NA` casting between base types
description:
Closes #451 

- Integer -> Logical `NA` casting is now supported
- Double -> Logical `NA` casting is now supported
- Character -> Logical `NA` casting is now supported
- A bug was fixed in detecting if a cast was `lossy` or not in the R level `vec_cast()` fallbacks. Before, you'd get this error due to `out != x` returning `NA`:

``` r
vctrs::vec_cast(matrix(NA_real_), matrix(NA_integer_))
#> Error in if (!any(lossy)) {: missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
```

If you have suggestions on how to simplify the `lossy` condition, I'm all for it. It took me awhile to parse.

- I added tests for all relevant `NA` conversions, and shaped `NA` conversions. The latter have the nice side effect of testing the R level casting functions. Fleshing it out this way helped me find all of the locations where we might not be handling `NA` casts correctly.

While I was there, I cleaned up some formatting and changed `Rf_isVector()` -> `vec_is_vector()`.

title: Add `.name_spec` support in `vec_c()`
description:
I didn't modify `vec_cbind()` as it might interfere with #446.

From our Slack discussion:

By default, outer names can only be combined with scalars or empty vectors:

```r
vec_c(foo = 1)
#>foo
#>  1

vec_c(foo = integer())
#> integer(0)
```

It is an error to provide both an outer name and a named vector:

```r
vec_c(foo = c(a = 1))
#> Error: Can't merge the outer name `foo` with a named vector.
#> Please supply a `.name_spec` specification.
```

And an error to provide an outer name and a length > 1 vector:

```r
vec_c(foo = 1:3)
#> Error: Can't merge the outer name `foo` with a vector of length > 1.
#> Please supply a `.name_spec` specification.
```

To get out of these errors, you can supply a glue specification:

```r
vec_c(foo = c(a = 1), bar = 1:3, .name_spec = "{outer}__{inner}")
#> foo__a bar__1 bar__2 bar__3
#>      1      1      2      3
```

You can also supply a function, if the inner vector is unnamed `inner` is character, otherwise it is integer:

```r
my_merge <- function(outer, inner) {
  if (is_character(inner)) {
    paste0(outer, "__", inner)
  } else {
    paste0(outer, inner * 10)
  }
}

vec_c(foo = c(a = 1), bar = 1:3, .name_spec = my_merge)
#> foo__a  bar10  bar20  bar30
#>      1      1      2      3
```

Lambda formulas are supported:

```r
vec_c(foo = 1:3, .name_spec = ~ .x)
#> foo foo foo 
#>   1   2   3 
```

Another application of this will be the vctrs-powered flatten functions:

```r
flatten(list(foo = list(a = 1, b = 2)), .name_spec = "{outer}_{inner}")
#> $foo_a
#> [1] 1
#>
#> $foo_b
#> [1] 2
```

```r
#> Error: Lossy cast from `x$a$b` <character> to `to$a$b` <double>.

```

I'm not sure about the last commit which adds default argument tags to `vec_cast()`. It improves the messages above (`to$a$b` instead of just `a$b`), but this looks slightly suboptimal in the non-nested case because of the repetition of "to":

```r
vec_cast("foo", 10.5)

```

Closes #57 and #225. 
Case 1 in #225 isn't solved, but I don't think we can make it better for this release.

title: Native array slicer
description:
A native `vec_slice()`r for arrays. I'll document in full tomorrow, but initial tests are promising! ~It doesn't quite work right with vctrs objects, but hopefully we can figure that out easily. I probably don't have something wired up correctly.~ (Update: falling back to `vec_slice_fallback()` when required)

I have changed `slice_names()` to return the sliced names rather than assign them directly. I need to use it to slice row names.

``` r
library(vctrs)
library(ggplot2)
library(magrittr)

# Short 1D array (select half of the rows)
x <- 1:10
dim(x) <- 10L

bench::mark(vec_slice(x, 1:5), x[1:5, drop = FALSE], iterations = 100000)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 10
#>   expression   min     mean   median    max `itr/sec` mem_alloc  n_gc n_itr
#>   <chr>      <bch> <bch:tm> <bch:tm> <bch:>     <dbl> <bch:byt> <dbl> <int>
#> 1 vec_slice… 893ns   1.29µs   1.25µs 45.8µs   773623.    6.45KB     8 99992
#> 2 x[1:5, dr… 371ns 517.39ns    499ns 41.8µs  1932768.        0B     8 99992
#> # … with 1 more variable: total_time <bch:tm>

# Medium sized matrix (selecting all rows)
z <- matrix(1:1000, nrow = 500)
idx <- 1:500 + 0L

bench::mark(vec_slice(z, idx), z[idx, , drop = FALSE], iterations = 100000)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 10
#>   expression    min   mean median    max `itr/sec` mem_alloc  n_gc n_itr
#>   <chr>      <bch:> <bch:> <bch:> <bch:>     <dbl> <bch:byt> <dbl> <int>
#> 1 vec_slice… 2.28µs 2.99µs 2.68µs 6.52ms   334311.    3.95KB     9 99991
#> 2 z[idx, , … 2.15µs 2.78µs 2.67µs 5.25ms   360133.    3.95KB     9 99991
#> # … with 1 more variable: total_time <bch:tm>

# (125000, 4, 2) double array
y <- 1:1000000 + 0
y <- array(y, c(length(y) / 8, 4, 2))

short_results <- bench::press(
  length = c(1, 10, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000),
  {
    idx <- seq_len(length) + 0L
    bench::mark(
      vec_slice(y, idx),
      y[idx, , , drop = FALSE],
      iterations = 100000
    )
  }
)

short_results %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = length, y = median, color = expression)) +
  geom_line() +
  ggtitle("Short index test")
```

title: Construct `base::order()` call with `expr()`
description:
Closes #356 

This failed because we were trying to attach the `base::order()` arguments to the unnamed data frame, which had 0 rows.

```
> vec_sort(data.frame())
Error in `$<-.data.frame`(`*tmp*`, "decreasing", value = FALSE) : 
  replacement has 1 row, data has 0
```

Instead, I now construct the `base::order()` expression with `expr()`, using `!!!` for the unnamed data frame.

This results in the following behavior:

``` r
library(vctrs)

vec_order(data.frame())
#> NULL

# consistent with order() called with no `...` args
# because that is essentially what happens, but maybe we want something
# different?
order()
#> NULL

vec_sort(data.frame())
#> data frame with 0 columns and 0 rows

vec_order(data.frame(x = numeric()))
#> integer(0)

vec_sort(data.frame(x = numeric()))
#> [1] x
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
```

I feel like it might be appropriate for `vec_order(data.frame())` to return `integer(0)`, but I think the only way to do that is an early exit if `vec_size(x) == 0`

title: Alter `vec_as_index()` signature
description:
Closes #381 

- `vec_as_index()` has changed from `vec_as_index(i, x)` -> `vec_as_index(i, size, names = NULL)`. This more accurately captures the required information used in this function, and makes it generic enough to work over any dimension, rather than just the first dimension.

- `vctrs_as_index()` is now a required function at the C level (because of the `size` arg), and has become the new bridge function between C and R.

- Two new tests were added regarding input validation for `size` and `names`.

- Internal C level naming consistency was improved by this PR. Rather than using `vec_n` or `data_n` for `vec_size(x)`, now only `size` is used.

- I added a check to `chr_as_index()` to ensure that `names` is a character vector (if not already caught by the `NULL` check). Since `names` is now an argument the user can pass in, this felt like an appropriate check.

- I added a `vec_assert()` for `size` at the R level to ensure that it is a length 1 integer.

I have tested this in rray, and it solves the issue raised in #381.

It feels appropriate to export `vec_as_index()` in a separate PR, so I will do that after this gets merged.

Question: I currently use `size` as the new argument name, which is consistent with how it is used in vctrs, but for rray I technically pass in the length of any dimension here. Should it just be `n`? If so, it will require a bit of renaming at the C level since we currently use `n` in many places for the index length.

Question: Should `names` default to `NULL`? They are only required when `i` is character and it felt odd repeatedly specifying it as `NULL` in the tests when `i` was not a character.

* `vec_repair_names()` is a shortcut for `set_names(x, vec_names(x))`.

* The original `vec_names()` function has been renamed to `vec_bare_names()`.

title: Implement `vec_rbind()` in C
description:
Performance is now closer too dplyr for small vectors, and scales better than dplyr.

```r
library(vctrs)
library(dplyr)
library(data.table)

bench <- function(data) {
  bench::mark(
    dplyr = bind_rows(!!!data),
    vctrs = vec_rbind(!!!data)
  )[1:6]
}

# For lists of data frames, includes data.table
bench2 <- function(data) {
  bench::mark(
    dplyr = bind_rows(!!!data),
    vctrs = vec_rbind(!!!data),
    data.table = rbindlist(data),
    check = FALSE
  )[1:6]
}

# Run manually with r-lib/vctrs@d7f2a72f0f
bench_before <- function(data) {
  bench::mark(
    before = vec_rbind(!!!data)
  )[1:6]
}
```

### Small vectors

```r
data <- rep(list(rlang::set_names(letters)), 10)
bench(data)
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>

bench_before(data)

```

Much faster than dplyr.

```r
bench_before(data)
```

title: Precache dictionary hashes
description:
This way the hashes can be computed with the vectorised method.

```r
x <- 1:1000

bench::mark(
  before = vec_hash(x, rowwise = TRUE),
  after = vec_hash(x, rowwise = FALSE),
  check = FALSE
)[1:6]

#>   <chr>      <bch:tm> <bch:tm> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl>
#> 1 before       22.8µs   37.2µs   33.8µs   1.16ms    26851.
#> 2 after        11.7µs   17.7µs   13.8µs  888.9µs    56583.


df <- tibble(x = 1:1000, y = 1000:1)

bench::mark(
  before = vec_hash(df, rowwise = TRUE),
  after = vec_hash(df, rowwise = FALSE),
  check = FALSE
)[1:6]
#>   expression      min     mean   median      max `itr/sec`
#>   <chr>      <bch:tm> <bch:tm> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl>
#> 1 before       83.6µs  103.7µs   87.3µs    736µs     9645.
#> 2 after        18.8µs   25.7µs   21.6µs    690µs    38915.


nested_df <- tibble(x = 1:1000, y = tibble(z = 1:1000))

bench::mark(
  before = vec_hash(nested_df, rowwise = TRUE),
  after = vec_hash(nested_df, rowwise = FALSE),
  check = FALSE
)[1:6]
#>   expression      min     mean   median      max `itr/sec`

#> 2 after        18.8µs   28.2µs   22.1µs    701µs    35450.
```

The hashes are also always precomputed, even in `_any` functions that could be short-circuited. This makes the code simpler and the best case performance gain of not prehashing doesn't seem to outweigh the other costs:

```r
worst <- 1:1000

best <- c(1L, 1L, 3:1000)

bench::mark(

)[1:6]

  check = FALSE
)[1:6]
#>   expression       min     mean   median      max `itr/sec`
#>   <chr>       <bch:tm> <bch:tm> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl>
#> 1 after_worst     28µs   34.1µs  28.86µs    633µs    29350.
```

title: Use tidy names in `vec_c()`
description:
Closes #271 

I compared `vec_c()` with `vec_c/rbind()` and realized it might benefit from the use of `tibble::tidy_names()`, which could solve #271. If you don't want this, no harm done. I'll add some tests if you like the idea.

This also alters the current way the names are built up in `vec_c()`. If any of the inputs are named, then any of the _unnamed_ inputs get `""` as their default name until `tibble::tidy_names()` can fix that. This is a similar approach as `vec_cbind()` I believe.

You can now do the following, which previously were errors:

``` r
library(vctrs)
library(rray)

# adds names to unnamed input
y <- 1
names(y) <- "a"
vec_c(y, 1)
#> New names:
#>  -> ..2
#>   a ..2 
#>   1   1

# works on matrices
x <- matrix(1:2, dimnames = list(letters[1:2], "c1"))
vec_c(x, 1)
#> New names:
#>  -> ..3
#>     [,1]
#> a      1
#> b      2
#> ..3    1

# - works on vctrs_vctr types
# - duplicate names are deduped
# - note that vec_c() also loses shape names (col names here)
mat <- rray(1, dim = c(1, 1), dim_names = list("r1", "c1"))
vec_c(mat, 2, mat)
#> New names:
#> r1 -> r1..1
#>  -> ..2
#> r1 -> r1..3
#> <vctrs_rray<double>[,1][3]>
#>       [,1]
#> r1..1    1
#> ..2      2
#> r1..3    1
```

<sup>Created on 2019-04-03 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1.9000)</sup>

title: Fix `vec_count()` with 3D+ arrays
description:
For whatever reason, base R flattens data frame "array columns" of dimensionality 3+ when you try and subset rows of the data frame with `[`. It doesn't do this for matrix columns. Luckily, `vec_slice()` does the right thing, so I replaced a call to `[` with `vec_slice()` to reorder rows in `vec_count()`.

``` r
library(vctrs)

vec <- c(1, 1, 5, 2, 2, 5)

# fine
vec_1d <- array(vec)
vec_count(vec_1d)
#>   key count
#> 1   2     2
#> 2   1     2
#> 3   5     2

# fine
mat <- array(vec, c(3, 2))
vec_count(mat)
#>   key.1 key.2 count
#> 1     1     2     2
#> 2     5     5     1

# flattened
arr_3d <- array(vec, c(3, 2, 1))
vec_count(arr_3d)
#>   key count
#> 1   1     2
#> 2   5     1

# flattened
arr_4d <- array(vec, c(3, 2, 1, 1))
vec_count(arr_4d)
#>   key count
#> 1   1     2
#> 2   5     1
```

Expected result you get with the fix:

``` r
library(vctrs)

vec <- c(1, 1, 5, 2, 2, 5)

# flattened
arr_3d <- array(vec, c(3, 2, 1))
vec_count(arr_3d)
#>   key.1 key.2 count
#> 1     1     2     2
#> 2     5     5     1

# flattened
arr_4d <- array(vec, c(3, 2, 1, 1))
vec_count(arr_4d)
#>   key.1 key.2 count
#> 1     1     2     2
#> 2     5     5     1
```

title: `vec_slice()` fails when slicing shaped objects by name
description:
The following currently fails:

``` r
library(vctrs)

x <- matrix(1:2)
dimnames(x) <- list(c("foo", "bar"))

vec_slice(x, "foo")
#> Error: Can't use character to index an unnamed vector.
```

I know eventually shaped object slicing will be incorporated fully, but this might be a general solution for `chr_as_index()`.

title: Optimization) `shape_broadcast()`
description:
I've noticed that sometimes `shape_broadcast()` can be an expensive function to call when it often doesn't need to be. With the following:

```
library(vctrs)

x <- matrix(1:10000) + 0L
y <- matrix(1:10000) + 0L

vec_cast(x, y)
```

- 3 copies are made on 3.5.2 (1 from `dim(x)<- dim_x`, and two from the final `[` call)
- 2 copies are made on 3.6.0 (the `dim(x)<- dim_x` copy is ALTREPed away)

For this example, I really think it should be much cheaper to call `vec_cast()`, so this PR makes two changes:

- If the shape of `x` and `y` are the same, return `x` early
- If the dimensionality of `x` does not change, do not set the dim of `x`

The first change helps on 3.5.2 and 3.6, the second change probably only helps on 3.5.2 but I don't think it hurts.

title: Add `vec_structure()` for use in `new_vctr()`
description:
Closes #341 

- New `vctrs_set_attributes()`, inspired heavily from `do_attributesgets()`, which removes all attributes from `x` and then adds the `attrib`.
   - All attributes must be named.
   - `dim` is always set first, consistent with `do_attributesget()` to avoid an issue of attempting to set dim names on a non-array object if the user does `vec_structure(x, dimnames = list(...), dim = c(...))`
   - Exposed as `vec_set_attributes()`

- New `vec_structure()` that tries to do the same thing no matter what R version you are on. Both versions try to first remove attributes of `.data`, then add the new ones.

- `new_vctr()` now uses `vec_structure()` and just passes `names` through rather than calling `attributes(.data) <- list(names = nms)` separately.

- `vec_data()` now uses `vec_set_attributes()`.

Questions)

- I'm setting `r_version` in the `.onLoad()` because it's actually quite slow to call `getRVersion()`. Is this right?
- Does `vctrs_set_attributes()` do what you were intending?
- Is there a better way to avoid having to switch off the r version? Maybe register these in `.onLoad()` rather than storing the R version?
- I can add tests, I guess specifically for `vec_set_attributes()`?

title: Implement `vec_slice<-` in C
description:
And add a `vec_assign()` variant that doesn't modify the input in the current environment.

Atomic assignment:

```r
bench::mark(
  before = vec_assign_before(letters, 1:15, ""),
  after = vec_assign(letters, 1:15, ""),
  base = base_assign(letters, 1:15, "")
)[1:6]
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 before      13.36µs  16.81µs    55647.      256B     11.1
#> 2 after        2.42µs   2.71µs   321932.      256B      0
#> 3 base         1.56µs   1.92µs   486901.      256B     48.7
```

Data frame assignment:

```r
df <- mtcars
val <- mtcars[1, ] * rnorm(ncol(mtcars))

bench::mark(
  before = vec_assign_before(df, 1:15, val),
  after = vec_assign(df, 1:15, val),
  base = base_row_assign(df, 1:15, val),
  check = FALSE # row.names currently not assigned
)[1:6]
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 before      103.5µs  115.1µs     8246.    3.27KB     15.1
#> 2 after        24.1µs     28µs    34065.    3.27KB     10.2
#> 3 base         71.7µs   81.7µs    11461.    3.27KB     15.2
```

Nested data frame assignment:

```r
nested <- tibble(nested = mtcars, !!!mtcars)
nested_val <- tibble(nested = val, !!!val)

bench::mark(
  before = vec_assign_before(nested, 1, nested_val),
  after = vec_assign(nested, 1, nested_val),
  tibble = base_row_assign(nested, 1, nested_val),
  check = FALSE
)[1:6]
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 before      194.9µs  212.4µs     4465.    6.53KB     12.8
#> 2 after        47.5µs   52.4µs    18084.    6.53KB     13.3
#> 3 tibble      115.7µs    128µs     7492.    6.53KB     15.4
```

Before the C implementation of cast and type2 for data frames, the above was much slower:

```r
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 before        906µs   1.08ms      883.    6.53KB     15.4
#> 2 after         738µs 842.69µs     1113.    6.53KB     15.3
#> 3 tibble        117µs 131.73µs     6848.    6.53KB     17.9
```

In general it seems essential for performance to implement cast and type2 in C to avoid dispatch. For instance, here are the results for factors, which are still implemented in R:


title: Redesign use of proxy and restore in internals
Handle names and coercion in argument tags
description:
This PR fixes support for names and coercions in `vec_type_common()` error messages. Ideally these two issues would be implemented in different PRs, unfortunately it would be hard to untangle the development history.

#### Coercion

The error message is currently confusing when an argument was coerced along the way:

```r
vec_type_common(1, TRUE, "chr")
#> Error: No common type for `list(...)[[2]]` <double> and `list(...)[[3]]` <character>.
```

One way to fix this would be to describe the coercion pattern:

```r
#> Error: No common type for `list(...)[[2]]` <double> coerced from <logical> and `list(...)[[3]]` <character>.
```

However this would be hard to implement with recursive data structures like data frames. A simpler solution is to keep track of the argument corresponding to the current type:

```r
#> Error: No common type for `list(...)[[1]]` <double> and `list(...)[[3]]` <character>.
```

To support this, `vec_type2()` now takes an output parameter `int* left` that indicates if the common type comes from the LHS or the RHS. It returns 1 for the LHS, 0 for the RHS, and -1 when both types are the same. The last value means that the LHS is taken as the default when `left` is coerced to a boolean.


#### Names

This PR also adds support for names:

```r
vec_type_common(foo = 1, bar = "")
Error: No common type for `foo` <double> and `bar` <character>.

vec_type_common(foo = df1, bar = df2)
#> Error: No common type for `foo$x$y$z` <double> and `bar$x$y$z` <character>.
```

The implementation is a bit more complicated than I expected because of the need to keep track of counters within splice boxes. When I first implemented `vec_type_common()` with `rlang::dots_values()` to avoid copies on splicing, I did not realise this would introduce such complexity later on. Not sure it was worth it in the end:

```r
many <- rep(list(1.5, 1:10), 1000)
bench::mark(
  dots_values = vec_type_common(!!!many),
  dots_list = vec_type_common_splice(!!!many)
)[1:6]
#>   expression       min     mean   median      max `itr/sec`
#>   <chr>       <bch:tm> <bch:tm> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl>
#> 1 dots_values    224µs    280µs    229µs 732.52µs     3572.
#> 2 dots_list      276µs    352µs    299µs   1.45ms     2842.
```

title: Fix fallback to `[`
description:

title: Introduce coercible-cast for assigning into vectors
description:
Makes `[<-`, `[[<-`, and `vec_slice<-` type-stable and closes #140.

Type-stability is ensured by casting after checking that the LHS and RHS types are coercible. If we just cast the RHS to the LHS, we have:

```r
x <- 1:2
vec_slice(x, 1) <- "10"
x
#> [1] 10  2

x <- c("foo", "bar")
vec_slice(x, 1) <- 10
x
#> [1] "10"  "bar"
```

With coercible-cast, we have:

```r
x <- 1:2
vec_slice(x, 1) <- "10"
#> Error: No common type for `x` <integer> and `value` <character>.

x <- c("foo", "bar")
vec_slice(x, 1) <- 10
#> Error: No common type for `x` <character> and `value` <double>.
```


The following used to work but is now an error:

```r
l <- list_of(1, 2, .ptype = int())
l[[1]] <- list(TRUE)
#> Error: No common type for `x` <double> and `value` <list>.
```

It should be one of these instead:

```r
l[1] <- list(TRUE)
l[[1]] <- TRUE
```

title: Include `vec_type_common()` index in argument tags
description:
```r
vec_c(df1, df1, df2)
#> Error: No common type for `list(...)[[2]]$x$y$z` <double> and `list(...)[[3]]$x$y$z` <character>.
```

Laziness is introduced to avoid an expensive generation of tags / manipulation of global buffers (the index would have to be formatted at each iteration). The laziness also makes it easy to enlabel user inputs without cost in the future, if we want to.

Methods that might fail no longer take a `const char*` as `arg` parameters. Instead, they take an object with `fill()` method which will generate the string when needed.

Memory management of the string buffer is done by allocating a RAWSXP with R. If it is too small, it is reallocated and the tag generation is repeated until success (or R throwing if the stack is full). I use low tech `memcpy()` idioms to manipulate the C strings, as suggested [here](https://stackoverflow.com/a/4689766/1725177) and other places. The caller always manages memory, and the callee get a pointer and a remaining size. A negative value should be returned if the buffer is too small. This way there is no truncation and no buffer overflow. This should be safe and I think the code is readable.

title: Fix unspecified casts
description:
* `vec_unspecified_cast()` is renamed to `vec_default_cast()`. In most cases it should be used in default methods instead of `stop_incompatible_cast()`. This reduces the amount of boilerplate necessary to implement a vector class.

* Default `vec_cast()` methods for bare types now use `vec_default_cast()` to allow unspecified casts.

* The integer64 default method reimplements `vec_default_cast()` manually because that class doesn't support `na_int` indexing, which throws off `vec_na()`.

* For lists the cast is different for `NA` vectors and unspecified vectors. It seems that `vec_cast(uns, list())` should be the same as `vec_na(list())`, i.e. use `NULL` as the missing value. This makes it different from `vec_cast(NA, list())` which returns `list(NA)`.

It might be possible to apply the same strategy to `vec_type2()` and export a default method to reduce the boilerplate.

title: Set `dim` attribute before any names in default `vec_restore()` method
description:
I hit a weird bug with the default `vec_restore()` method that has to do with how R treats names of 1D arrays. Here's the minimal example:

``` r
library(vctrs)

x <- array(c(1, 2), dimnames = list(c("nm1", "nm2")))
x
#> nm1 nm2 
#>   1   2

# `names` attribute is actually set?
vec_restore(x, matrix(1))
#> nm1 nm2 
#>   1   2 
#> attr(,"names")
#> [1] "nm1" "nm2"
```

A bit of exploring shows that R treats `names` special for 1D arrays

``` r
library(vctrs)

x <- array(c(1, 2), dimnames = list(c("nm1", "nm2")))
x
#> nm1 nm2 
#>   1   2

# only dimnames
attributes(x)
#> $dim
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> $dimnames
#> $dimnames[[1]]
#> [1] "nm1" "nm2"

# but this registers names
names(x)
#> [1] "nm1" "nm2"

# so does this
attr(x, "names", exact = TRUE)
#> [1] "nm1" "nm2"

# no problems here
vec_restore(x, 1L)
#> nm1 nm2 
#>   1   2

# `names` attribute is actually set?
vec_restore(x, matrix(1))
#> nm1 nm2 
#>   1   2 
#> attr(,"names")
#> [1] "nm1" "nm2"

x_2D <- as.matrix(x)
x_2D
#>     [,1]
#> nm1    1
#> nm2    2

# no problem here
vec_restore(x_2D, matrix(1))
#>     [,1]
#> nm1    1
#> nm2    2
```

I think what is happening on the vctrs side is that the default `vec_restore()`:

- Collects the `R_NamesSymbol` from `x` as `nms`, which is actually a thing for 1D arrays, but otherwise returns NULL for 2D+ structures.
- Calls `SET_ATTRIB(x, attrib)` which sets `dim = c(1,1)`, so its now 2D
- Calls `Rf_setAttrib(x, R_NamesSymbol, nms);`, which actually sets the names attribute with `nms` for a matrix. Great. If this was a 1D array still, I think it would skip over it and wouldn't set the `"names"` attribute directly.
- Then `Rf_setAttrib(x, R_DimSymbol, dim);` restores the 1D dimensionality.

I think that _ideally_ `SET_ATTRIB(x, attrib)` call wouldn't set incorrect attributes to begin with (meaning it shouldn't have used the names, dim, and dimnames of `to`, which immediately get overwritten anyways).

The easiest alternative solution is implemented here. I just set the `R_DimSymbol` first so that the setting of the `R_NamesSymbol` is skipped over.

description:
This untangles dispatch to `[` and dispatch from `[`.

* When `vec_slice()` is called with an S3 object, we fall back to `[` instead of slicing the `vec_proxy()` so we're immediately compatible with foreign types.

* Our own types implement `[` methods which call `vec_slice_native()`. The latter is a variant that turns off the `[` fallback. In this case, the `vec_proxy()` is sliced.

We'll probably want to special-case the vctrs classes in the S3 branch of `vec_slice()` to avoid the `vec_slice()` -> `[` -> `vec_slice_native()` -> `vec_proxy()` dance. Perhaps the C extension mechanism would be a good way to do so. We'll also need to export `vec_slice_native()` so third party classes can call `vec_slice()` from their `[` methods. This helper will probably need to handle dimensionality.

title: Fix array restoration

title: Add `vec_proxy()` and implement size and slice genericity with proxies
description:
Closes #124.

* New `vec_proxy()` generic. This should become the main customisation point in vctrs. It only needs to be implemented when the base type of a vector class is not its own data.

* Use `vec_proxy()` in `vec_slice()` and `vec_size()` to handle S3 vectors.

title: Install older highr to fix 3.1 CI
Make `vec_slice()` generic
description:
* `vec_slice()` is now a generic. The default method dispatches to `[`.

* A new dispatch implementation allows (a) masking its arguments and (b) forwarding dots if they exist in the generic environment. Dispatch now occurs in the generic environment instead of the global env to make it easier to mask and to forward dots.

* New `vec_slice_bare()` function that is not a generic. This can be used to call `vec_slice()` from `[` methods without inflooping dispatch. `vec_typeof()` gains a `vec_typeof_impl()` variant as well to support this. It has a `dispatch` argument that disables `vctrs_type_s3`.

* Call `vec_slice_bare()` and `vec_slice()` from the `[` methods for `vctr` and `rcrd` types. Because `vec_slice()` preserves attributes, the constructor for `vctr`, called from `vec_restore()`, now allows (but ignores) attributes.

title: Implement `vec_slice()` in C
description:
New `vec_as_index()` function that transforms an index vector (missing, character, logical or integer) to an integer vector of positions. The semantics are identical to those of base R subsetting:

* Negative indices are inverted.
 * Zeros are filtered out.
* Logical vectors are recycled, including `NA`.
* Bounds are checked. OOB is an error.

`vec_as_index()` is currently unexported but should eventually make it easier to implement subsetting for custom classes because only one type of indices needs to be dealt with. Internally, it will avoid the recomputation of the index for each component when a composite structure such as a data frame or a record type is sliced.

The C implementations of slicing have these features:

* Missing values are propagated on slice and ignored on slice-assign.
* Unlike base R, attributes of unclassed structures are reproduced.

title: Typos and vignette proofreading
description:
I really enjoyed reading vignettes of this package and can't wait for it to reach "stable" lifecycle. Along the way found these improvement opportunities. Sorry for mixing in one PR code and vignette updates.

Extra thoughts:

- In 's3-vector.Rmd' vignette [there is a description](https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/4d848c977556d19af320e9dbfd2a3487eb62999b/vignettes/s3-vector.Rmd#L820) about arithmetic between meters and numbers. I would argue that only both multiplications and division by a number are acceptable, as, strictly speaking, meter and number are object of different nature and can't be used with `+` and `-`.
- In 'stability.Rmd' vignette `c()` [is called length-stable](https://github.com/echasnovski/vctrs/blob/1b165d0c0e78634a3dace8e649a793a4a2fd9a95/vignettes/stability.Rmd#L90) (using "always") with [later attempt](https://github.com/echasnovski/vctrs/blob/1b165d0c0e78634a3dace8e649a793a4a2fd9a95/vignettes/stability.Rmd#L169) to rightfully refute this. That is an attempt, because it doesn't actually show the breaking behaviour (see [pkgdown site](https://vctrs.r-lib.org/articles/stability.html#non-vectors)), so extra objects in global environment needed. Maybe it is better to use "almost length-stable" in the examples and [later "Data frames" section](https://github.com/echasnovski/vctrs/blob/1b165d0c0e78634a3dace8e649a793a4a2fd9a95/vignettes/stability.Rmd#L274)
